_note: Tranche F. Forty five surahs written in parallel by nine writers working from the house schema and the evidence rules, then audited by three readers who did not write them. The audit returned no fabricated citations and seven factual inaccuracies, every one of which was corrected before this file was written: a misattributed verse in Al-Hijr, a wrong claim about which surahs share Alif Lam Ra, an overstated superlative in Ash-Shu'ara, a virtue graded sunnah whose own text said no reward is promised, a miscounted verse span in At-Tur, a narrator attribution in Al-Insan, and a word count in Al-Qiyamah.

context: Al-An'am is Makkan and belongs to the last stretch of the Makkan years, when the argument with Quraysh had hardened and neither side expected the other to move. Its audience acknowledged Allah as creator and still assigned Him partners, and they had built a law of their own around livestock and crops: portions set aside for their gods, animals whose backs were declared forbidden, unborn young reserved for the men and denied to the women.

That setting explains the method. Al-An'am does not preach so much as litigate, and the command Say is issued to the Prophet ﷺ dozens of times, each one handing him a sentence for a specific objection. Cattle, which give the surah its name, arrive only from verse 136, by which point the ground is prepared: if Allah alone creates, provides and knows, nobody else has standing to declare a camel unlawful.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from the an'am, the grazing livestock, taken up in the closing third where the surah lists what Quraysh had invented: crops divided between Allah and partners, cattle dedicated so that an idol's name was spoken over them, the eight pairs argued through at verses 143 and 144. Naming a surah of sustained theology after farm animals keeps attention on where the theology was meant to land.

movements.note: The surah praises the One who made the darknesses and the light, then turns to generations already destroyed and to the scene where those who denied the meeting ask to be sent back.

movements.h: It is not you they deny
movements.note: The Prophet ﷺ is told the rejection is not aimed at him, with earlier messengers as precedent. Verse 59 holds the keys of the unseen, alongside the order not to drive away the poor who call on their Lord morning and evening.
A star, then the moon, then the sun, each rejected as it sets. Ibrahim then heads a list naming eighteen prophets in four verses, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to follow their guidance.

movements.h: They did not appraise Him rightly
movements.note: The splitting of the seed, the stations of the sun and moon, and the warning at verse 108 against insulting the idols of others, since the insult comes back.
How a false religion is built, through embellished talk passed between people, and then the practices themselves: harvests divided with partners, children killed out of poverty, cattle set aside.

Against their list, a real one. Verses 151 to 153 set out what is prohibited and name this the straight path, and the surah closes by assigning prayer, sacrifice, living and dying to the Lord of the worlds.

themes.d: The case for one God is built from premises the Makkans already accepted, which is why the surah keeps asking who provides, who hears, who owns the night.
Twice, at verses 12 and 54, Allah is said to have decreed mercy upon Himself, and both statements sit inside passages about denial and ruin rather than at the end.

themes.t: The limits of what people know
themes.d: With Him are the keys of the unseen, and no leaf falls without His knowledge. Ignorance becomes the reason to stop legislating: people who cannot see a seed split have no basis for forbidding an animal.

What a person eats and forbids is treated as the visible test of what he believes about God. Jurists later differed over the details, including meat slaughtered without the name of Allah being said over it.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-An'am assumes that belief is something a person can reason toward and then live from. Its pace is deliberate and it rarely raises its voice. A reader who takes it in long sittings notices how often it answers an objection nobody has raised yet, which is a way of clearing ground ahead of a person's own doubts.

Two passages tend to stay. The first is Ibrahim under the night sky, rejecting each light as it sets, a mind reaching tawhid without a teacher. The second is verse 162, where prayer, sacrifice, life and death are handed over in one sentence. Both appear in the supplication that opens the prayer, reported from the Prophet ﷺ by 'Ali in Sahih Muslim 771a.

passages.why: The keys of the unseen, the falling leaf, the grain in the darkness of the earth. Nowhere else does the surah measure so plainly the distance between what Allah knows and what anyone else can reach.
Ibrahim's conclusion once the star, the moon and the sun have set. The wording belongs to the opening supplication of the prayer in Sahih Muslim 771a.
What is genuinely forbidden, answering a list people invented. It runs from associating partners with Allah to killing children out of poverty, and closes by naming the path.
Prayer, sacrifice, living and dying assigned in one line. Short enough to hold in memory and wide enough to summarise the surah.

connections.why: Al-A'raf follows immediately and takes the same argument into history, showing what became of the towns that decided otherwise.
An-Nahl returns to the invented prohibitions and names the fault outright, warning against tongues that assert this is lawful and this is unlawful.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-An'am. What circulates instead concerns the manner of its revelation, that it came down complete at night escorted by seventy thousand angels, recorded by at-Tabarani and in another wording by al-Hakim; the critics differ over those chains, and in any case they say nothing about a reward for reciting. Its standing rests on its content, the longest sustained argument for tawhid revealed in Makkah.
virtue.src: no virtue-of-recitation report; the revelation report in at-Tabarani 12/215 and al-Hakim 2/314, grading disputed

context: Al-A'raf is Makkan and is the longest surah revealed before the hijrah. Most authorities place it late in that period, close to Al-An'am, when the Prophet ﷺ had been preaching for years in a town that had settled into refusal. To people in that position it gives a long look backwards at five other towns that refused, and then at Pharaoh, who refused with an army behind him.

The shape follows from that. More than half its length is narrative, and the narratives are arranged as one case file: Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb receive short parallel entries in almost identical wording, after which Musa receives some seventy verses. Repetition is the argument. By the time Pharaoh speaks, a reader recognises the lines, because five other peoples have already said them.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from verses 46 to 49, where a group stands on the heights between the Garden and the Fire, seeing both sides and knowing the people of each by their marks. Who they are is not stated, and the commentators differ. Naming the surah after them rather than after Adam or Musa keeps a reader inside its central concern, the weighing announced at verse 8.

movements.h: The scales and the first refusal
movements.note: The Book is sent down, the destroyed towns are recalled, and the scales are set for the Day. Then Adam: the refusal of Iblis, the whispering, the tree, and the exposure that follows.

Repeated addresses to the children of Adam, on clothing, on the adornment to be taken at every place of prayer, and on the enemy who stripped their parents. The nations then argue with one another in the Fire.

Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb, each sent to his own people, each denied, each community removed. Verse 96 names the alternative: had the towns believed, blessings would have been opened from the sky and the earth.
The staff, the contest with the magicians, and the magicians prostrating and then threatened with mutilation and crucifixion. Plagues follow in sequence, and then the sea.

movements.h: The mountain, the tablets, the calf
movements.note: Musa asks to see his Lord and the mountain is levelled. He returns to find the calf, and the surah turns to the covenant of Israel, the unlettered Prophet ﷺ described in their scripture, and the Sabbath-breaking town by the sea.

The covenant taken from the offspring of Adam, the man who shook off the signs he was given, and the finest names. Verse 204, on listening when the Qur'an is recited, is cited in the schools' long disagreement over reciting al-Fatihah behind an imam.

themes.d: Five prophets are given nearly the same speech and receive nearly the same answer. The wording repeats on purpose, so the outcome reads as a rule and not as a run of local misfortunes.
Adam's account turns on being stripped, and the address to his children immediately after is about garments, including the garment of mindfulness at verse 26.
A group belonging to neither party yet able to see both is unusual in the Qur'an, and it gives the surah somewhere to stand, since everything before has been about which way a life tips.
At verse 172 the descendants of Adam are brought out and asked whether He is their Lord. The passage removes the plea of inherited ignorance rather than explaining an event.

heart: This surah asks to be read in long stretches, because its effect depends on accumulation. A page a day makes the Nuh section a story and nothing more. Taken in one sitting, the five towns begin to work, the near identical sentences arriving again and again until a reader stops wondering what happened to Thamud and starts watching the mechanism.

Then the ending changes register. After two hundred verses of nations and armies, the last lines narrow to one person: hold to pardon, enjoin what is right, turn away from the ignorant, and when the whisper comes, remember. The final verse is a place of prostration, the first in the order of the mushaf.

passages.why: The words Adam and his wife said afterwards, the first repentance recorded in the Qur'an and the pattern for the rest: naming the wrong as one's own before asking for anything.
Musa asks to see his Lord and the mountain is levelled. The verse sets the limit of what is given even to a messenger in this life.
The covenant taken from all the descendants of Adam. Readers return to it because it makes belief a matter of recognition rather than acquisition.
Hold to pardon, enjoin what is right, turn away from the ignorant. An ethic of conduct in one line, at the end of a surah about civilisations that failed.

connections.why: Ash-Shu'ara tells the same run of prophets in compressed form with a refrain, delivering the same material at a different speed.
Ta-Ha gives Musa at close range, including the conversation at the fire that Al-A'raf passes over in a few words.

virtue.text: No report states a reward for reciting Al-A'raf. What is established is the practice of the Prophet ﷺ: Zayd ibn Thabit objected to short surahs being recited at Maghrib and said he had seen the Prophet ﷺ recite in that prayer the longer of the two long ones, in Bukhari 764, and an-Nasa'i 990 names that surah as Al-A'raf. The report fixes a practice and promises nothing.
virtue.src: Bukhari 764, from Zayd ibn Thabit; an-Nasa'i 990 names the surah as Al-A'raf

context: Al-Anfal is Madinan and belongs to the weeks after Badr, fought in Ramadan of the second year after the hijrah. The sirah accounts put roughly three hundred Muslims against about a thousand of Quraysh, with some seventy of the enemy killed and about as many taken captive. When the fighting stopped the men disagreed over the captured goods: those who had chased the enemy, those who had stayed around the Prophet ﷺ and those who had held the line each had a claim.

Almost everything in it follows from a battle won against the odds and nearly spoiled afterwards. Verse 17 takes the victory out of the victors' hands, verse 41 regulates the property, verses 67 to 69 correct the handling of the captives, and the middle section is given to the discipline that made the day possible. It reads less like a commemoration than like a debrief conducted by the One who decided the outcome.
surahs.name_story: Al-Anfal means the spoils, and the surah is named for the question that began it: they ask you about the anfal. The answer at verse 1 divides nothing; it reassigns ownership, saying the spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger, and only at verse 41 does a rule of distribution appear. Naming the surah after the quarrel rather than the victory records where the community stood.

movements.note: The quarrel over spoils is answered with a description of the believers, then the memory of setting out unwillingly and a thousand angels sent in support. Verse 17 removes the killing and the throwing from human credit.

Instructions on answering when the Messenger ﷺ calls, on a trial that will not fall only on wrongdoers, and on wealth and children as a test, with a reminder of the days when the believers were few and feared being snatched away.

movements.h: The fifth, and the day of the criterion
movements.note: A rule for a fifth of what is taken, and the naming of Badr as the day the two parties met. Jurists differ over how the fifth is divided after the Prophet ﷺ, particularly the shares named for him and his relatives.

Stand firm, remember Allah, obey, and do not quarrel among yourselves. The stretch covers broken treaties, the instruction to prepare what force can be prepared, and the command to incline to peace when the other side inclines.

The reproach over the captives taken at Badr, then a word addressed to those captives. Emigrants and helpers are bound to one another at the close, and blood relatives are given their standing in the decree of Allah.

themes.d: You did not kill them, but Allah killed them, and you did not throw when you threw. The sentence comes before the rules, so what follows is legislation for people just told the win was not theirs.
Firmness, remembrance and obedience are the instructions for meeting an enemy, and the ban on quarrelling carries a physical consequence: courage goes and strength departs.
The answer to a fight over goods is to put the goods under Allah and His Messenger before dividing anything. Jurists later differed over how the opening verse relates to the fifth at verse 41.
The closing verses bind emigrants and helpers to each other as protectors, and verse 75 then restores the priority of blood relatives. A new solidarity is built without abolishing the old one.

heart: Al-Anfal is short and its tone stays level. It came to people who had just done something extraordinary and were arguing about the proceeds, and it neither congratulates them nor scolds them at length. A reader coming to it after a success of his own will notice how quickly the credit is moved elsewhere.

The line most readers keep is the one about not quarrelling, which names the cost of internal dispute in physical terms and sits in the middle of battle instructions. It belongs to a surah that opened with a quarrel over property, so the two ends explain each other.

passages.why: The believers described by what happens inside them: hearts that stir at the mention of Allah, faith increased when His verses are recited, reliance on Him.
You did not kill them, but Allah killed them, and you did not throw when you threw. The Qur'an's clearest statement that a human act and a divine act can occupy the same moment.
Respond to Allah and the Messenger when he calls you to what gives you life. The verse then says Allah comes between a person and his heart.
Do not quarrel with one another, or you will lose heart and your strength will depart. A short account of why communities right about everything else still fail.

connections.why: Al 'Imran covers Uhud, the battle that followed and reversed this one. Together they give both halves of one instruction about crediting results.
At-Tawbah carries on the subject of treaties and their ending, and follows Al-Anfal in the mushaf without the usual opening formula between them.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Anfal. What is transmitted concerns its placement: Ibn Abbas asked Uthman why Al-Anfal and Bara'ah were joined without the Bismillah between them, and Uthman answered that their subjects resembled one another and that he took them for one surah. Those are a companion's words, not a prophetic report, and the critics differ over the chain, at-Tirmidhi's version graded hasan and Abu Dawud's graded weak.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; Uthman's account in at-Tirmidhi 3086, graded hasan, and Abu Dawud 786, graded weak

context: Yunus is Makkan and opens with the letters Alif Lam Ra, which it shares with Hud and Yusuf, the two surahs that follow it. The demand it answers is recorded at verse 15: bring a Qur'an other than this one, or change it. Behind that stood two fixed positions, that revelation should not come to an ordinary man among them, and that the idols were brokers who would speak on their worshippers' behalf.

Because the objection was to the Qur'an rather than to a doctrine, much of the surah is about the Qur'an: where it came from, why it cannot be exchanged, what it does to a person who receives it. The narratives arrive late and are chosen for one purpose. Nuh, then Musa, then the people of Yunus answer a question about timing, which is how long a refusal can run before it can no longer be withdrawn.
surahs.name_story: The surah carries the name of a prophet who appears in one verse, 98, and whose story is not told here at all. That verse is the reason. No town believed and had its faith benefit it, the surah says, except the people of Yunus. Every other community named in these pages is an instance of refusal, so naming the whole surah after the one exception states what it wants remembered.

movements.note: The objection to revelation reaching a human being, the ordering of the sun and the moon, and the man who calls on his Lord while lying on his side and walks on once relief comes.

Passengers in a good wind meet a wave from every side and call on Allah alone, promising gratitude. Worldly life is then compared to rain that greens a field before the harvest is taken, and the challenge to produce a single surah like it follows.

movements.h: Healing, and the friends of Allah
movements.note: Some listen and some look, and neither helps without willingness. The Qur'an is named an instruction and a healing for what is in the breasts, and those close to Allah are described as people over whom no fear comes.

Nuh tells his people to settle their plans and act, his own affair being already committed. Musa follows, with the magicians, the houses turned into places of prayer, and Pharaoh declaring faith as the water closes over him.

The close states that had the Lord willed, everyone on earth would have believed, and asks the Prophet ﷺ whether he would then compel them. It ends by telling him to follow what is revealed and wait for Allah to judge.

themes.d: Pharaoh's faith is refused at the moment of drowning in verse 90, and eight verses later the people of Yunus are named as the only town whose faith arrived in time. Placing them so close together is the argument about deadlines.
The sea passage at verses 22 and 23 shows worship at its most sincere and its most temporary: distress produces a perfect monotheist, and relief undoes him within a sentence.

themes.t: A book that cannot be swapped
themes.d: The demand for a different Qur'an is met with a challenge to produce one surah like it, and with the statement that the Prophet ﷺ could not alter it of his own accord.
Verse 99 says that Allah could have made everyone on earth believe. It limits what a messenger is for, and rules out force before anyone has proposed it.

heart: Yunus is a calm surah about urgent things, and its recurring image is water: rain that greens a field and is then cut down, a sea that turns on a ship, a wave closing over an army. Recited slowly, these gather into one point about how quickly a settled situation stops being settled.

Most readers stop at the drowning. Pharaoh says the right words in the right order and is told it is too late, and verse 92 adds that his body will be preserved as a sign for those who come after. Six verses later the people of Yunus are named, who said much the same words earlier and were accepted. The distance on the page is short and the difference between the outcomes is timing.

passages.why: A ship in a fair wind, a wave from every side, and the promise made in the middle of it. The passage ends by noting what people do with such promises once the ground is firm again.
An instruction from your Lord and a healing for what is in the breasts. Here the Qur'an describes its effect on a person rather than its authority over him.
No fear will come upon the friends of Allah, nor will they grieve. Short and unqualified, and followed at once by a description of who is meant.
The one exception in the whole record of towns, the people of Yunus, who withdrew a refusal while withdrawal was still possible.

connections.why: As-Saffat carries the account of Yunus that this surah leaves out, the flight, the fish, and the sending back to a hundred thousand or more.
Hud follows immediately, opens with the same letters, and covers much of the same ground by narrative where Yunus covers it by argument.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Surah Yunus. What is authentically reported concerns the prophet rather than the surah: the Prophet ﷺ said that no servant should say he is better than Yunus ibn Matta, in Bukhari 3413 and in several other places in that collection. Nothing in it speaks about recitation, and the surah's standing rests on its content.
virtue.src: no virtue-of-recitation report; the report on Yunus ibn Matta, Bukhari 3413, concerns the prophet and not the surah

context: Hud is Makkan and is usually placed close to Yunus, with which it shares its opening letters and much of its material. It belongs to the years when the Makkan mission had produced a small, pressed community and no sign of a general change of heart. Its audience includes the Prophet ﷺ himself, who is told at verse 120 that these accounts are related to him in order to make his heart firm.

That stated purpose explains the shape. The surah is a run of long narratives, each told with more interior detail than its parallels elsewhere: Nuh arguing, then building, then calling to a son who will not board; Ibrahim watching guests whose hands do not reach the food; Shu'ayb refusing to exempt himself from what he asks of others. Hud is less interested in what the nations did than in what it cost the men sent to them.
surahs.name_story: Named for the prophet sent to 'Ad, whose section runs from verse 50 to verse 60 and is not the longest in it. The name marks the surah out, and it fits, because his speech carries its most concentrated statement of reliance: he has entrusted himself to the Lord who holds every creature by its forelock, said to people threatening him with the anger of their gods.

movements.h: A book set out in detail
movements.note: Verses made firm and then explained, an audience folding their chests to hide from the One who knows what they conceal, and the guarantee that every creature on earth has its provision.

movements.h: Nuh, and a son who would not board
movements.note: The mockery of a man building a ship, the oven bursting with water, and the boarding in the name of Allah. Nuh calls his son, who answers that he will climb a mountain, and afterwards is told the boy is not of his family.
'Ad denies and is removed after Hud tells them to plot against him without delay. Thamud hamstrings the she-camel and is given three days, after which the shriek takes them in their homes.

movements.h: Guests, and a town turned over
movements.note: Messengers reach Ibrahim with news of a son and of a town to be destroyed, and he argues for Lut's people until he is told to leave it. The town is overturned and rained with layered stones.
Madyan is addressed on short weights and full ones, and Shu'ayb says his success is only through Allah. Musa and Pharaoh follow briefly.

The Day when no one speaks except by permission, the order to remain upright and not lean toward wrongdoers, and prayer at the two ends of the day, where the commentators differ over which prayers the phrases designate.

themes.t: Told in order to steady someone
themes.d: Verse 120 gives the purpose of the narratives outright, which is to make the heart of the Prophet ﷺ firm. Few places in the Qur'an say what a story is for.

Shu'ayb wants nothing but reform as far as he is able, and verse 117 says the towns would not have been destroyed unjustly while their people were reformers. The word covers honest trade and correct worship together.
Nuh's son drowns and his father's plea is refused with the statement that the boy's conduct was not righteous. It is the hardest instance in the Qur'an of faith being neither inherited nor lent.
The command at verse 112 to remain upright is addressed to a man in the middle of a losing argument with his own town, and it is paired with prayer and patience rather than with relief.

heart: Hud is a heavy surah and it does not lighten. Its narratives end badly for nearly everyone in them and the few rescues are narrow. Slow recitation gives not comfort but company: a man asked to keep going is shown a line of others asked the same thing.

Near the close, something unexpected happens. After all the ruined towns comes an instruction to establish prayer at the two ends of the day, with the statement that good deeds remove bad ones. The occasion is reported in Bukhari 526 and Muslim 2763a: a man came to the Prophet ﷺ having done with a woman what he should not have done, the verse came down, and he was told it was not for him alone but for the whole community.

passages.why: There is no creature on earth but that its provision rests with Allah, who knows its dwelling and its place of storage. Placed early, before any of the destroyed towns.
Shu'ayb's answer to his people: he does not intend to differ from them in what he forbids, he intends reform as far as he is able, and his success is only through Allah.
Prayer at the two ends of the day, and the statement that good deeds remove bad ones. The occasion is recorded in Bukhari 526 and Muslim 2763a.
The Qur'an explaining why it tells stories, which is to make firm the heart of the one receiving them.

connections.why: Al-A'raf covers the same nations in the same sequence at shorter length. Comparing them shows what Hud adds, which is almost always the inside of the conversation.
Surah Nuh gives the flood from inside Nuh's own report of his preaching. The two supply the effort and its result.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a merit for reciting Surah Hud. The saying often quoted, that Hud and its sisters turned the hair of the Prophet ﷺ grey, is recorded in at-Tirmidhi 3297, where at-Tirmidhi calls it hasan gharib, and scholars have differed over its chains, some noting that certain routes do not reach the Prophet ﷺ in connected form. That disagreement is left as it stands here, and in any case the report describes the weight of what the surah says rather than promising anything to a reciter.
virtue.src: at-Tirmidhi 3297, graded hasan gharib by at-Tirmidhi and contested by others; not a report of recitation reward

context: Ibrahim is Makkan and was sent down to the people of a city Ibrahim had asked Allah to make secure, whose sanctuary and water they still lived off. They traced their descent to him, kept the pilgrimage he had established, and had filled the House he built with idols. Some early authorities read two of its verses as pointing to the Quraysh who fell at Badr, and that reading is disputed.

What follows is built out of speech: a Book sent down to bring people from the darknesses into the light, every messenger sent in the tongue of his own people, a good word compared to a rooted tree, and at the end Ibrahim speaking for seven verses. The founder of the city asks for exactly what his descendants had abandoned. He asks to be kept away from idols, and the people hearing this were standing among them.
surahs.name_story: Ibrahim does not appear until verse 35, and when he arrives he neither argues with anyone nor breaks anything. He prays. Naming a surah after a passage of supplication rather than a story is unusual, and it points a reader at the fact that the man who built the sanctuary spent his prayer worrying about idolatry among his own descendants.

movements.h: Out of the darknesses into the light
movements.note: The purpose of the revelation is stated in the first verse and repeated for Musa in the fifth, with the order to remind his people of the days of Allah. Verse 7 sets out the rule of increase for gratitude.

movements.h: The record of the earlier peoples
movements.note: Nuh, 'Ad and Thamud are named without their stories, and the exchange is reduced to essentials: a demand for proof, a threat of expulsion, a promise of the land to those who remain.

movements.h: Shaytan's speech, and the two trees
movements.note: Once judgement is passed, Shaytan denies holding any authority over his followers beyond an invitation they accepted. Then the good word as a tree with fixed roots and branches in the sky, and the corrupt word as a tree pulled up from the surface.

movements.h: The favours that cannot be counted
movements.note: Ships running at His command, rivers, the sun and moon in constant service, night and day, and the statement that the favours of Allah cannot be counted by anyone who tries.
Ibrahim asks for security for the city, for protection from idols, for hearts to incline toward the family left in a bare valley, and for prayer to be kept up by him and his descendants.
A warning against supposing Allah unaware of what wrongdoers do, the earth replaced by another earth, and a last verse describing the surah itself as a notification.

themes.t: Revelation as speech in a known tongue
themes.d: Every messenger was sent in the language of his people, given at verse 4 as a condition of making things clear. The surah keeps returning to words: the word that roots, the word that is torn up, the invitation Shaytan admits was only ever an invitation.
Verse 7 does not praise gratitude as a virtue but states it as a cause with an announced effect, naming the alternative in the same breath.
Shaytan's speech at verse 22 is a disclaimer after the fact: he called, they answered, and he asks them not to blame him.
Ibrahim asks to be kept from idols after a lifetime of breaking them, and asks the same for his sons, in front of an audience descended from him who had done exactly what he feared.

heart: Ibrahim is a short surah with an unusually steady voice. Nothing in it is narrated at length, and slow recitation works by accumulation rather than drama: light and darkness, a rooted tree and an uprooted one, favours beyond counting, a day on which eyes do not blink.

The part most readers carry is the supplication, which repays being read whole, because it moves outward in a definite order: the city, then protection from idols for himself and his sons, then the descendants left in the bare valley, then his parents, then all the believers. One verse of it, the line where Ibrahim says that whoever follows him is of him, was recited by the Prophet ﷺ before he raised his hands and wept for his community.

passages.why: If you are grateful, I will increase you. A condition stated plainly, with the consequence of the opposite named immediately after.
Shaytan's address to his followers once judgement is over, admitting he had no authority except that he called and they answered.
The good word as a good tree, its root fixed and its branches in the sky, giving fruit every season by the permission of its Lord.
Ibrahim asking to be made someone who keeps up the prayer, then asking forgiveness for his parents and the believers on the day of reckoning. The words are ancient and are still said.

connections.why: Al-Baqarah gives the same supplication at the House from another angle at verses 126 to 129.
Al-An'am shows Ibrahim reasoning his way to the One God as a young man. This surah shows him much later, asking that the conclusion hold in his children.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Surah Ibrahim. What is authentically recorded involves one of its verses rather than the surah: the Prophet ﷺ recited the words of Ibrahim at verse 36, then raised his hands, asked twice for his community and wept, in Muslim 202. That report says nothing about a reward for reciting, and the surah's standing rests on the supplication at verses 35 to 41.
virtue.src: no virtue-of-recitation report; the Prophet ﷺ reciting 14:36 and weeping for his community, Muslim 202

context: Al-Hijr is Makkan, and its opening does not address people hearing the message for the first time. The deniers have settled their position: they call the Prophet ﷺ mad at 15:6 and demand that angels be brought down at 15:7. At 15:3 he is told to leave them to their eating and their hopes, an instruction given about an argument that has stopped moving.

That deadlock explains why the surah declines to supply the sign it was asked for. If a gate of heaven were opened and they climbed through it all day, says 15:14, they would call it an illusion. So it turns to evidence of another kind. Thamud cut their houses out of rock and felt safe in them, and the ruined towns of Lut's people are noted at 15:76 as sitting on a road still in use.
surahs.name_story: Al-Hijr is the rocky tract in northern Arabia where Thamud cut dwellings into the cliffs, named once at 15:80. Out of ninety-nine verses covering the making of man, the refusal of Iblis and the night of Lut's people, the surah is called after a place, and one the first audience could reach by caravan.

movements.note: The disconnected letters, the demand for angels, and the statement that no community was destroyed before its known term. An opened gate of heaven would change nothing.
The sky given its great stars, the earth spread with everything growing in a weighed amount, and the fertilizing winds. At 15:21 nothing comes down except by a known measure.
Man shaped from dark clay and Iblis refusing to bow. He asks for time and gets it, then 15:42 fences what it buys him: no authority except over those who follow him.
The righteous enter gardens with whatever they carried of grudge taken out of their chests. Guests then arrive at Ibrahim's house with news of a son and an errand elsewhere.
Lut's people seized at sunrise, the companions of the thicket, and the companions of al-Hijr who cut homes from the mountains in safety. At 15:76 the sites lie on an established road.

movements.h: Seven verses, then the order to speak
movements.note: The gift of the seven oft-repeated, the instruction not to let the eyes travel over what others were given, and the command to proclaim openly. A constricted chest is answered with prostration.

themes.d: At 15:9 the safeguarding of the revelation is placed in the same hands that sent it down, at a stage when the text lived mostly in memory and on scattered materials.

themes.t: A delay is not a licence
themes.d: Iblis asks for time and receives exactly that. The surah grants the reprieve, then limits what it buys: he can invite and decorate, and he cannot compel.
The demand was for something from the sky. The answer is abandoned sites the audience passed on their own trade routes, shifting the burden to what they decline to look at.
The seven oft-repeated and the instruction to stop measuring against other people's provision both arrive before the order to preach in public. Consolation first, risk second.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-Hijr reads as a surah for a person whose chest has tightened. That condition is named in those words at 15:97, and what follows is not advice about the feeling but a list of actions: praise, prostrate, keep worshipping. Nothing is promised about the tightness lifting.

The other line readers keep is the last one. Worship your Lord until the certainty comes to you, with al-yaqin read by the great majority of commentators as death. That sets no interim target and attaches no condition, and somebody waiting for circumstances to improve finds the waiting quietly removed.

passages.why: The guarantee of the Qur'an's preservation, usually quoted alone. It sits among the objections of people calling the revelation a fabrication, which is what it answers.
What is taken out of the chests of the people of the Garden is named exactly: whatever they carried of resentment toward each other, removed before they sit facing one another.
The instruction not to let the eyes travel over what others were given, paired in one verse with lowering the wing to the believers. Two directions of attention.
The closing verse, setting the term of worship at the arrival of certainty. Short and unconditional, which is why readers return to it in stretches with no visible end.

connections.why: Al-A'raf carries the same dialogue with Iblis and the same run of destroyed nations at far greater length. Together they show what Al-Hijr compressed and how little the argument lost.
Hud tells the guests of Ibrahim and the night of Lut's people as full narrative. Al-Hijr covers both in under thirty verses, and the difference in pace is the comparison.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Hijr. What the surah has instead is one phrase the Prophet ﷺ explained himself: the seven oft-repeated of 15:87 are Al-Fatiha, as he told Abu Sa'id ibn al-Mu'alla in a report recorded by Bukhari. That identifies a phrase rather than attaching a reward to reciting this surah, and is given here as what it is.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; the seven oft-repeated identified as Al-Fatiha in Bukhari

context: Al-Hajj is counted Medinan in the standard classification, and it is one of the surahs where that classification has never fully settled. Early authorities differ over which verses belong to Makka and which came after the migration. The situation behind its middle section is not disputed: a community expelled from Makka, told to honour a House it could not reach.

That gap shapes the surah. It opens on the Hour, closes on the command to strive, and in between takes the pilgrimage back to its founding, with Ibrahim clearing the site of the House and calling out to people who did not yet exist. Permission to fight is given at 22:39, and the reason follows at 22:40: without one people being checked by another, monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques would be pulled down. Ibn Abbas is reported to have called 22:39 the first verse permitting fighting, a companion's statement rather than a prophetic report.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for the pilgrimage, and the naming is precise in an unexpected way. It legislates less of the hajj than a reader might expect, spending its central passage on the origin of the rite: the House cleared for those who circle it, the proclamation sent to every distant pass, and the offerings that reach nothing.

movements.h: The Hour, and a faith held at the edge
movements.note: The earthquake that makes a nursing mother forget her child, and human formation traced from dust to a lump of flesh. Then, at 22:11, the worshipper standing on an edge.
The House purified for those who circle and bow, and the pilgrimage proclaimed to people arriving on foot and on every lean camel. At 22:37, only the taqwa reaches Allah.
Fighting is permitted to those wronged and driven from their homes for saying that their Lord is Allah. The stated purpose lists monasteries, churches and synagogues before mosques.
No prophet was sent without something thrown into his recitation and then removed, which makes the interference a test rather than a defeat.

movements.h: Signs, and rites for every community
movements.note: The earth revived after rain, the sky held from falling, and ships running on the sea by His command. Each community was given rites of its own.

movements.h: The fly, then bow and strive
movements.note: Everything invoked besides Allah could not together create a single fly, nor recover what a fly took from them. The surah closes on bowing, prostrating and striving.

themes.d: The worshipper on an edge at 22:11 describes a failure that is not disbelief. Belief is present and conditioned on outcomes, and the surah sets it beside the Hour so a reader sees the load.
At 22:37 the surah removes any suggestion that the act itself reaches or feeds anything. The value stays in the state of the person performing it.

themes.t: A defence of other people's places of worship
themes.d: The permission to fight is given a purpose one verse later, and the first buildings named are not Muslim ones. Monasteries, churches and synagogues come before mosques.
Ibrahim is told to proclaim to people who are not there, and the same verse describes them arriving from every distant pass. The command was given to an empty valley.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-Hajj is uncomfortable in a way that turns out to be useful. It opens by describing what the Hour does to a nursing mother and does not soften the picture, then, with no transition, describes somebody worshipping on an edge. Readers who have noticed their own practice improving whenever life improves tend to stop there.

Two lines here get taken out on hard days. At 22:46 blindness is located in the chest rather than the eyes. The closing verse says the religion was not made narrow, and it arrives after seventy-seven verses of earthquake, expulsion and permitted war.

passages.why: The worshipper standing on an edge, at ease while good arrives and turning on his face at the first trial. The loss is named as both this world and the next.
Ibrahim told to call people to the pilgrimage, with the same verse describing them coming on foot and on every lean camel from every distant pass.
Neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah. The clearest statement in the Qur'an about what a rite is for, placed inside the passage prescribing the rite.
The eyes are not what goes blind. It follows an instruction to travel the land and look at what is left of earlier towns.

connections.why: Al-Baqara shows Ibrahim raising the foundations of the House and legislates hajj for a community that could not yet reach it. Al-Hajj goes back to the clearing of its ground.
Al-Fath came down on the return from Hudaybiyya, when the Muslims had been turned back within reach of the House. It shows what waiting for that access cost.

virtue.text: No report establishing a general merit for reciting Al-Hajj is authentic. The one regularly cited concerns its prostrations of recitation: 'Uqba ibn Amir asked whether Al-Hajj was favoured above other surahs with two of them and was told that it was. Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi both transmit it, its chain has been criticised, and graders differ between hasan and weak, so it is not presented here as established. The schools of law differ on the underlying question independently: Shafi'i and Hanbali jurists count two prostrations of recitation here, at 22:18 and 22:77, while Hanafi and Maliki jurists count only the first.
virtue.src: 'Uqba ibn Amir's report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi; grading disputed

context: Ash-Shu'ara is Makkan, and its third verse states the situation more plainly than any biography could: perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief that they will not believe. The address is to a man whose own city has refused him. At 227 verses it has more verses than any other Makkan surah, though Al-A'raf runs longer in actual length, and nearly all of it is narrative.

The setting explains the method. Rather than a new argument, the surah supplies seven earlier cases and tells five of them to a fixed pattern. Nuh, Hud, Salih, Lut and Shu'ayb each open with the same four sentences: I am a trustworthy messenger to you, so fear Allah and obey me, and I ask you no payment, my payment is only from the Lord of the worlds. Every episode closes with the same two lines about a sign most did not accept and a Lord who is the Mighty, the Merciful.
surahs.name_story: The poets appear only in the final four verses, and the surah is named after them. Placement is the point. After more than two hundred verses demonstrating what revelation sounds like, the closing answers the charge that the Prophet ﷺ was a poet of the ordinary sort, separating those who wander in every valley and say what they do not do from those who believe and act.

movements.note: The opening letters, and the grief of the Prophet ﷺ at their refusal named as a danger to him. A sign from heaven would leave their necks bent to it.

movements.h: Musa in the court and at the sea
movements.note: The call in the valley, the fear of being killed for an old death, and the exchange with Fir'awn about what the Lord of the worlds is. The magicians prostrate and are threatened with crucifixion.
The argument with his father over inherited idols, then Ibrahim describing his Lord as the one who feeds him, gives him drink and cures him. It ends in the request for a sound heart.
Three cycles in the fixed pattern. Nuh is told his followers are the lowest people, 'Ad are asked about their monuments on every high place, Thamud about the gardens they expect to keep.
The same pattern twice more. Lut's people are warned about an appetite no nation before them preferred, and the people of the thicket are told to give full measure.

movements.h: Where this came from, and who the poets are
movements.note: The Qur'an brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit onto the Prophet's heart in clear Arabic. It closes on the command to warn his nearest relatives, and the line drawn between poets and messengers.

themes.d: The sentence about wanting no wage is put in five different mouths. It is the one claim about a messenger an audience can check without settling a theological question first.
Ibrahim's request at 26:89 names the only asset that transfers. The verse before it rules out wealth and children, leaving the condition of the heart as the entire inventory.
The surah names the Prophet's distress in its third verse and never resolves it. What it supplies is seven men in the same position, none of whom persuaded his people either.
The closing does not deny that the recitation moves its listeners; it locates the source. The devils neither brought it down nor are able to, and poets say what they do not do.

heart: Recited slowly, this surah works by wearing a groove. The closing couplet arrives eight times and says the same thing: there was a sign in that, most did not accept it, and your Lord is the Mighty, the Merciful. Those two names sit together at the end of every account of a nation destroyed.

The passage most people keep is Ibrahim's, and what it does with illness rewards attention. He says of his Lord that He created him and guides him, feeds him and gives him drink, and then the construction shifts: and when I fall ill, He cures me. Falling sick is first person and the healing is not.

passages.why: The Prophet's grief at the refusal of his people, named and treated as a danger to him. Readers carrying responsibility for someone who will not listen return to it.
Ibrahim attributes falling ill to himself and the cure to his Lord, in a list where every other item is attributed to Allah alone. The shift is in the grammar.
Wealth and children named as the two things that will not help, with one exception: a heart brought sound. Ibrahim's whole supplication moves toward this and stops there.
The command to warn his nearest relatives. It is widely reported in Bukhari and Muslim that the Prophet ﷺ answered by climbing Safa and calling the clans of Quraysh by name.

connections.why: Ta-Ha tells the same encounter with Fir'awn from the inside, with Musa's fear and the private conversation at the valley given room. Ash-Shu'ara tells it as public confrontation.
Al-Qamar runs several of the same nations at a fraction of the length, each account closed by its own repeated refrain. It shows the identical material at maximum compression.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Ash-Shu'ara. Its standing rests on its content and on one well attested moment: when 26:214 came down, the Prophet ﷺ climbed Safa and called the clans of Quraysh by name, an incident recorded in both Bukhari and Muslim. That is an occasion of revelation rather than a merit of recitation.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; the Safa incident at 26:214 in Bukhari and Muslim

context: An-Naml is Makkan and sits between two surahs it shares material with, Ash-Shu'ara before it and Al-Qasas after it. All three open with disconnected letters beginning Ta Sin, and this is the shortest of them. Its first verses name the audience narrowly: guidance and good news for those who establish prayer, give the purifying due, and are certain about the Hereafter.

What separates it from its neighbours is that the account at its centre does not end in ruin. Sulayman's section runs about thirty verses and finishes with a queen entering Islam by her own decision, after an exchange of letters, a refused gift and a test with a floor of glass. Thamud and Lut's people are then set beside her, so both endings sit in one place.
surahs.name_story: The surah takes its name from one ant at 27:18, who warns her colony to get into their dwellings before Sulayman's armies crush them without noticing. Sulayman, given the speech of birds and command over jinn, men and birds, hears her and smiles, and the first thing he says is a request to be enabled to give thanks.

movements.note: The letters, the Qur'an described as a clear Book, and the naming of who it reaches. Guidance is something belief receives rather than something that produces belief.
He sets out to fetch a burning brand for his family and finds himself spoken to. Nine signs go to Fir'awn, and 27:14 records that they were rejected by people inwardly certain of them.

movements.h: Sulayman, the ant, the hoopoe, the queen
movements.note: Knowledge given to Dawud and Sulayman, the ant, and the hoopoe returning with news of a people prostrating to the sun. Then the letter, the refused gift, the throne fetched, and the queen's words on the glass floor.

movements.h: Two towns that would not be argued with
movements.note: Salih among a people split into two disputing factions, and the nine men who swore by Allah at night to kill him. Then Lut, whose people mocked a family for keeping itself clean.
Five parallel questions beginning at 27:60, covering creation, the water that grows gardens, the barrier between the two seas, the answer given to the desperate, and provision from sky and ground.

movements.h: The Hour, and the mountains that move
movements.note: The unseen kept with Allah alone, the creature brought out of the earth, and the blast of the trumpet. Near the close, mountains a person would call fixed pass like cloud.

themes.t: Power measured by what it notices
themes.d: The surah hands Sulayman every instrument of dominance, then spends its most memorable verses on him overhearing an insect and questioning a bird that failed to report.
At 27:14 the surah says outright that Fir'awn's people rejected the signs while their own selves were convinced, naming the causes as wrongdoing and arrogance rather than a shortage of evidence.
The queen of Saba is not frightened into faith. She takes counsel, tests Sulayman with a gift, travels to see for herself, and states her decision in her own words at 27:44.

themes.t: The answer given to the desperate
themes.d: The middle of the five questions names its subject as the one pressed until no option is left, describing prayer from the side of a person who has run out.

heart: Recited slowly, An-Naml changes texture more than most surahs, and the shifts are what a reader notices first. Long stretches of dialogue between kings, birds and councillors give way at 27:60 to five short parallel questions that end the same way each time. Reciters often slow at 27:62, on the one who answers the distressed.

The image the surah leaves last is worth carrying. Mountains anyone would swear are fixed are described passing like cloud, at the end of a surah that has spent its length on thrones, armies, a letter and a palace floor of glass. Everything solid turns out to have been in motion.

passages.why: Sulayman smiles at the ant and then asks to be enabled to give thanks for what was given to him and to his parents. A request for gratitude rather than for more.
The throne arrives before a glance can return, brought by someone identified only as having knowledge from the Scripture. Sulayman calls it a test of whether he will be grateful or ungrateful.
The verse names its subject as the one pressed to the point of having nothing left, and the answer described is given to that person specifically.
Mountains that appear rigid passing like clouds. Placed inside the account of the Day, it makes the permanence of the ordinary world a matter of how things look.

connections.why: Saba appears here at its height, with a throne, a council and a queen who submits. Surah Saba shows the same nation generations later, after the dam broke and the gardens turned to bitter fruit.
Sad gives Dawud and Sulayman a longer treatment, with each tested and each turning back to his Lord. An-Naml pairs the two in one sentence about knowledge.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting An-Naml. The surah holds one distinction of text rather than reward: 27:30 is the only place the Bismillah appears inside a surah rather than at its head, quoted as the opening line of Sulayman's letter. The schools of law differ over whether the Bismillah counts as a verse of the surahs it heads, a separate question from this verse, which is reported speech inside a narrative.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report

context: Al-Ankabut is Makkan by the standard classification, though early authorities differ over the opening, with some holding that the first ten or eleven verses came after the migration. The situation it addresses is not in dispute. People had said they believed and were being hurt for it, and 29:10 describes others who said the same, then treated persecution by human beings as though it were punishment from Allah, and turned back.

That is why the surah opens with a question about assumption rather than an argument about God. Before a single prophet is named, it states that being left alone after a declaration of faith was never the arrangement, and that earlier generations were tested so the truthful and the lying would be made evident. Everything after that reads as case material assembled for the opening claim.
surahs.name_story: The spider appears once, at 29:41, as a comparison for anyone taking protectors besides Allah: like a spider that has taken a house, and the flimsiest of houses is the spider's house. The comparison is not about how a web is built, which is intricate enough, but about what it keeps out, which is nothing.

movements.note: The opening question about being left alone after saying we believe, answered by the testing of those before. It includes the instruction on parents that stops short of obeying them into shirk.

movements.h: Nuh's long years and Ibrahim's fire
movements.note: Nuh among his people for a thousand years less fifty. Ibrahim argues that what they worship cannot provide for them, his people propose he be burned, and he leaves with Lut.
Lut's people, Madyan, 'Ad and Thamud whose dwellings were still visible, then Qarun, Fir'awn and Haman. At 29:40 the methods are listed separately: stones, a blast, the earth swallowing, drowning.
The comparison, and the note that such examples are grasped only by people with knowledge. It ends with the instruction to establish prayer, because prayer restrains from indecency and wrongdoing.

movements.h: How to argue, and what the Book already is
movements.note: Dispute with the People of the Scripture only in the better way, except with those among them who do wrong. The Prophet ﷺ recited no scripture before this and wrote none by hand.
His earth is spacious, every soul tastes death, and creatures carrying no provision of their own are fed. People call on Allah sincerely at sea and associate others once ashore.

themes.d: The surah's first move removes the idea that a statement of faith buys exemption from difficulty. Framing it as a question locates the error in expectation rather than in doctrine.
At 29:12 the deniers offer to bear the sins of anyone who follows them. The next verse cancels the offer and adds that they will carry their own burdens and others besides.

29:45 claims what the prayer does rather than what it earns: it restrains from indecency and wrongdoing. Placed four verses after the spider, it supplies the shelter the alternatives failed to provide.

themes.t: Sincerity that surfaces only in emergencies
themes.d: The passage about the ship describes people whose religion is entirely real while the danger lasts and gone once they are ashore, which the surah treats as mistaking a web for a house.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-Ankabut is a surah for the middle of a hard stretch rather than the end of one. It makes no promise that the difficulty will lift. What it removes instead is the interpretation that difficulty means something has gone wrong, and it does that in the first three verses.

The final verse is the one most readers keep, and its wording repays slowing down. Those who strive for Us, We will guide them to Our ways. Guidance is placed after the striving rather than before it, and the ways are plural, which suggests more than one route being opened. Nothing is said about the destination arriving sooner.

passages.why: The opening question and its answer. It names the assumption most people bring to a declaration of faith and takes it away in two verses, with earlier generations as the evidence.
The spider's house, called the flimsiest of houses. The comparison works because a web is a real structure that catches real things and stops nothing that would matter.
Prayer described by what it prevents rather than by what it earns, closing with the statement that the remembrance of Allah is greater.
The closing promise, conditioned on striving and worded as guidance to ways in the plural. Readers return to it when effort has not yet produced anything visible.

connections.why: Al-Baqara asks the Medinan version of the same question at 2:214, whether people supposed they would enter the Garden without what came to those before them.
Luqman repeats this surah's ruling on parents, that they are accompanied with kindness and not obeyed into associating anything with Allah, placing it inside a father's advice to his son.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Ankabut, and nothing in the reliable collections attaches a reward to it in particular. Its standing rests on its own content: an opening that states in three verses the principle that a declaration of faith is followed by testing, and two of the most quoted verses in the Qur'an on prayer and on effort, at 29:45 and 29:69.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report

context: Saba is Makkan and opens with praise, joining the small group of surahs that begin that way. Its audience had been told the Hour was coming and answered with a taunt the surah quotes at 34:7: shall we point you to a man who tells you that once you have been torn to pieces you will be made new again.

The answer chosen is not philosophical. Two households given more than anyone else are held up, Dawud's and Sulayman's, then a nation given two rows of gardens and safe short stages of travel, and the surah shows what became of all three. Iron softened in the hands, wind covering a month in a morning, and a king found dead leaning on a staff that only a crawling creature had noticed.
surahs.name_story: Saba was a kingdom in the south of Arabia, and the surah is named for it because the account at 34:15 to 21 is the cleanest instance of the argument the whole surah makes. Two gardens, one on the right and one on the left, an instruction to eat from the provision and give thanks, and a land called good under a Lord who forgives. Then the flood of the dam.

movements.note: Praise for what is in the heavens and the earth and for the Hereafter as well, then the denial of the Hour. At 34:3 the answer is a measure: not an atom's weight escapes Him.
Mountains and birds repeating the praises with Dawud, iron made soft in his hands, and jinn working before Sulayman. His death goes unnoticed until a creature eats through his staff.

movements.h: The two gardens and the dam
movements.note: Saba given a sign in their own dwelling place, told to eat and give thanks, and turning away. The flood arrives, the short safe stages are replaced, and they are made into stories.

movements.h: Nothing you call on owns an atom
movements.note: The challenge to invoke whatever is claimed besides Allah, and the denial that any of them hold a share in the heavens or earth. Intercession is limited to what He permits.
The exchange between those who were led and those who led them, each turning on the other. The affluent of every warned town claim wealth exempts them, and 34:37 corrects it.
The single instruction, to stand for Allah in twos and singly and then think it over, followed by the refusal of any wage. It ends with people seized where there is no escape.

themes.d: The family of Dawud are told at 34:13 to work in gratitude, and the same verse observes that few of His servants are grateful. Saba receive the same instruction two verses later and do not follow it.
The measure appears at 34:3 for what cannot escape Allah's knowledge and again at 34:22 for what the objects of worship do not own. One unit establishes His reach, then their emptiness.
The affluent of every warned town drew the same conclusion from their prosperity, that comfort meant approval. At 34:37 the surah names faith and righteous work as what closes the distance.

themes.t: Stand, in twos and alone, and think
themes.d: 34:46 reduces the surah's whole demand to one instruction, and it is procedural rather than doctrinal. It asks for a posture and an act of reflection, and nothing further.

heart: Recited slowly, Saba is about how quickly a settled world stops being settled. Both long narratives end in an undoing nobody present saw coming. The jinn went on working for a king already dead. A nation that could move between its towns in safety asked for the distances to be lengthened, and was scattered.

The line most readers carry sits at the end of 34:13, a short clause following a description of favour without parallel: and few of My servants are grateful. Its placement does the work, arriving at the peak of the account of what was given rather than at the moment of loss.

passages.why: The family of Dawud told to work in gratitude, followed immediately by the observation that few of His servants are grateful, at the height of the account of what they were given.
A people asking for the stages of their travel to be made longer, when the short safe stages were the favour. The verse records the request, the self-wronging and the scattering in one line.
Wealth and children ruled out as what brings a person nearer, with the verse then naming what does. It answers an inference the surah has just quoted the affluent making.
The whole demand reduced to one instruction: stand for Allah, in twos and one by one, and then think. Nothing else is asked in the verse.

connections.why: An-Naml shows Saba at its height, with a queen, a throne and a council, ending in her submission. This surah shows the same nation after the dam gave way.
Al-Kahf tells of a man with two gardens who was certain they would never perish, and who was left turning his hands over in regret. Saba gives the same image at the scale of a nation.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Saba. It is not among the surahs the Prophet ﷺ is recorded as singling out for any time, prayer or occasion, and that absence is the accurate finding rather than a missing piece. The surah's standing rests on its argument, which uses Sulayman's court and the gardens of Saba to show how little it takes for an established order to come apart.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report

context: Fatir is Makkan, from the years when refusal in Makkah had hardened into a settled position. It opens by praising Allah as Originator of the heavens and the earth, who made the angels messengers with wings in twos and threes and fours, and it addresses a city that had heard the argument and decided against it.

That setting explains its balance. Little space goes to debating the resurrection and a great deal to what Allah does without interruption: sending winds, opening a mercy nobody can withhold, holding the heavens and the earth in place. Against that, the Prophet ﷺ is told he is only a warner, and told not to let his soul waste away in grief over them.
surahs.name_story: The name is the first word after the praise, Fatir, from a root meaning to split something open, which is how the Qur'an describes the heavens and the earth being brought into being. An older name for the surah is Al-Mala'ika, the Angels, taken from the same verse. Both point at one line, and that line sets the terms: the question is who originates and who sustains.

movements.note: Praise of the Originator, angels given wings, and a mercy He opens that none can hold back. Then the warning against being deceived about Allah, and the instruction to treat Shaytan as the enemy he is.

movements.h: What rises and what owns nothing
movements.note: Winds driving clouds to dead land, honour declared to belong wholly to Allah, and the good word that ascends with the righteous deed lifting it. What they call on besides Him does not own the membrane on a date stone.

movements.h: You are the ones in need
movements.note: Humanity addressed as the poor before the Free of need, then the rule that no bearer of burdens carries another's. Four pairs are set out as unequal: blind and seeing, darkness and light, shade and heat, living and dead.

movements.h: Colours, and three kinds of heir
movements.note: The differing colours of fruits, mountains, people and beasts, ending on the line that it is those with knowledge who fear Allah. Then the Book inherited by three sorts of people, and a cry from the Fire answered with a question about years already spent.
Their oaths that they would be better guided than any earlier nation, and the plot that closes on its own authors. Allah holds the heavens and the earth lest they cease.

themes.d: The address at verse fifteen goes to all people and not to the deniers alone: you are the ones in need of Allah, and Allah is the Free of need.

themes.t: Words go up, deeds carry them
themes.d: To Him ascends the good word, and the righteous deed raises it. Speech and action are one motion here, and the verse follows a line about honour sought in the wrong place.
Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah. The verse ends a passage on the colours of fruits and mountains, which locates the knowing meant: attention to what is in front of a person.
The Book is inherited by one who wrongs himself, one who is moderate, and one foremost in good deeds. All three sit inside the group described as chosen.

heart: Recited slowly, this is a surah for someone carrying weight that was never assigned to them. Its steadiest move is to remove responsibility for outcomes while leaving the work in place. You are not but a warner. No bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another.

A slow reading also surfaces the list of what happens whether or not anyone notices. Winds are moved, clouds driven to dead ground, fresh water and salt kept apart, the heavens held in position. Beside that, verse fifteen reads differently: O mankind, you are those in need of Allah, while Allah is the Free of need.

passages.why: So let not worldly life delude you, and let not the Deceiver deceive you about Allah. Two deceptions in one verse, and the second is much harder to notice.
O mankind, you are those in need of Allah, while Allah is the Free of need. Addressed to everyone, which is why it stops believers as often as deniers.
Those who recite the Book of Allah, establish prayer and spend secretly and openly expect a transaction that will never perish. The commercial word is the Qur'an's own.
The cry from the Fire asking to be sent back, answered with a question about years already given. Time spent, rather than mercy refused.

connections.why: Saba sits immediately before it and opens with the same praise, and the two run one argument about ownership and provision at different speeds.
Ar-Rum builds its case from winds, rain and dead earth revived, the same evidence Fatir uses, which shows how standard the method was in Makkah.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Fatir. Its standing rests on content: it is one of the surahs that opens by praising Allah, and the one that opens by naming Him the Originator. Verse twenty nine carries a promise about recitation, but it is made to those who recite the Book of Allah in general rather than to readers of this surah.
virtue.src: no authentic virtue report

context: As-Saffat is Makkan, from the stage when the argument had turned contemptuous. The deniers are quoted saying that once they are dust and bones they will not be raised, and that the man addressing them is a poet possessed. Instead of answering in the abstract, the surah walks into the next life and lets the reader hear people talking there.

That decision shapes everything. Its Fire is where followers and the men they followed argue about whose fault it was. Its Garden holds a man who remembers a colleague who mocked him. At each prophet the surah runs the same two lines: thus do We reward the doers of good, and peace upon the one just named.
surahs.name_story: As-Saffat is taken from the opening oath, by those ranged in ranks, and the phrase is left unexplained for well over a hundred verses. Near the end the ones sworn by speak for themselves: there is not among us any except that he has a known station. The naming ties the surah's two ends together.

movements.h: The oath and the guarded sky
movements.note: The ranks, the drivers and the reciters are sworn by, before the declaration that your God is One. The nearest heaven is guarded against every rebellious devil trying to listen in.

Mockery of the resurrection, then the exchange in which followers blame the men they followed and are told they were never believers. Against it, the cup passed in the Garden, white and pleasant, with no loss of sense in it.
One of the people of the Garden remembers a companion who thought the resurrection absurd, asks to look, and sees him in the middle of the Blaze. Then the tree of Zaqqum.
Nuh called and was answered. Ibrahim asks his people what they worship, strikes their idols, is thrown into a furnace, and is then shown the vision of the sacrifice.

movements.h: Four more, and the same two lines
movements.note: Musa and Harun given the clarifying Scripture, Ilyas asking why his people call on Ba'l, Lut delivered while the rest were destroyed, and Yunus cast onto open ground while ill.
The claim that the angels are daughters of Allah is put back to the deniers. The angels answer for themselves about their stations, and the surah closes with peace upon the messengers.

themes.t: A refrain instead of an argument
themes.d: After Nuh, after Ibrahim, after Musa and Harun, after Ilyas, the same sentence returns: thus do We reward the doers of good. Repetition turns four accounts into one claim.

themes.t: The next life has conversation in it
themes.d: People here speak after they are raised. They blame one another, ask to look over an edge, and make requests that are refused. The Hereafter is populated, not silent.
Ibrahim tells his son what he has been shown and asks what he thinks. The reply comes with no bargaining, and the ransom arrives only after both had submitted.
The angels describe themselves as each holding an assigned position. Order runs from the guarded sky in the opening verses through to the last accounting.

heart: Recited slowly, the passage on Ibrahim is where most readers stop, and it is remarkably short. He says he has seen in a dream that he is to sacrifice his son, then asks the boy what he thinks. The boy answers: do as you are commanded, you will find me, if Allah wills, among the patient.

The refrain does the rest. Read at speed it passes as a formula. Read slowly, four times over, it becomes a statement about how this account of the world is arranged: someone reaches the end of what they can manage, they hold, and the same sentence follows.

passages.why: The exchange between father and son. The father asks for the boy's view before acting, and the boy answers in one sentence with no conditions.
And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. One verse, and the yearly sacrifice of the Muslims recalls it.
There is not among us any except that he has a known position. Spoken by the angels, and it is the surah explaining its own title.
Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe, and peace upon the messengers. Three verses long used to close a gathering.

connections.why: Al-Anbiya gathers more prophets into less space and without a refrain, so reading the two together shows what the repetition adds.
Al-Hajj sets out the rites recalling this ransom, and says that neither meat nor blood reaches Allah, only the taqwa of the one offering.

virtue.text: No authentic prophetic report establishes a specific merit for reciting As-Saffat. Its closing three verses are widely used to end a gathering, a practice with long usage behind it rather than an established prophetic instruction. One caution belongs with it: the Qur'an does not name the son in the sacrifice, and the early commentators divided over whether it was Isma'il or Ishaq. This companion leaves the question there.
virtue.src: no authentic virtue report

context: Sad is Makkan and its opening is tied to a scene the early sources report from Ibn Abbas, recorded by Ahmad and by Tirmidhi. Abu Talib had fallen ill, and Quraysh chiefs came to complain to him about his nephew. The Prophet ﷺ asked them for one word, saying that by it the Arabs would submit to them, and when he named it, la ilaha illa Allah, they stood and walked out.

The first seven verses quote that walkout close to the way it happened, including the instruction the chiefs gave each other to hold to their gods. What follows answers men who refused on grounds of standing rather than evidence, and it ends with the first refusal in creation, made by Iblis on the same footing: I am better than him.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for the single letter that opens it, Sad, followed by an oath by the Qur'an full of reminder. No explanation of the letter is offered and the classical commentators did not settle on one. What the name leaves at the threshold is an unexplained sound, in front of a surah whose opening scene is men refusing one sentence.

movements.note: The oath by the Qur'an, the chiefs walking out over the demand that the gods be one, and their complaint that they had heard nothing like it in the religion they knew. A short roll of earlier peoples follows.

movements.h: The two men who climbed the wall
movements.note: Dawud given strength, with mountains and birds exalting alongside him. Two litigants come over the wall of his chamber with a case about ninety nine ewes and one, he judges, understands he has been tested, and falls down.

The heavens and the earth were not made in vain, and the Book was sent down so its verses would be considered. Then Sulayman: the horses brought out in the afternoon, and his request for a kingdom suiting nobody after him.

movements.h: The ones who kept coming back
movements.note: Ayyub is told to strike the ground with his foot, a spring comes up, and his family is restored. A list of chosen servants follows: Ibrahim, Ishaq, Ya'qub, Isma'il, Al-Yasa' and Dhul-Kifl.

movements.h: Two houses, and a quarrel inside one
movements.note: Gardens of perpetual residence with their gates thrown open, set against arrivals in the Fire who curse each other and ask why they cannot see men they used to count among the worst.
Adam formed from clay, the angels prostrating, and the refusal of Iblis on the argument that fire outranks clay. He is granted respite and swears to mislead all except the sincere.

themes.d: The word applied to Dawud, to Sulayman and to Ayyub does not mean faultless. It describes someone who keeps coming back, and each time it follows a scene where something had gone wrong.
The chiefs will not accept one god because accepting costs them standing. Iblis will not bow because he reads his own material as superior. Both refusals are about status.
Dawud is a king who receives a judgment against himself. Sulayman is a king whose throne has something set on it. Power is a situation to be handled, not a reward.

themes.t: A Book meant to be considered
themes.d: A blessed Book We have revealed to you that they might reflect upon its verses. Deliberation is the stated purpose of revelation, a reproach to men who would not weigh one sentence.

heart: Recited slowly, Sad is a surah about men who went down and did not stay down. Dawud realises in the middle of a judgment that the case was about him, and the next thing recorded is that he fell prostrate and turned in repentance. Ayyub gets four words as the verdict on years the surah never narrates.

There is a reason readers keep this surah's verbs rather than its scenes. Returning, seeking forgiveness, falling down, coming back again. The last figure in it did none of these, and he knew exactly who was speaking to him.

passages.why: Dawud understanding that he himself was the matter under judgment, and going down. A short distance between recognising a fault and acting on it.
A blessed Book We have revealed to you that they might reflect upon its verses. One of the clearest statements the Qur'an makes about what it is for.
We found him patient, an excellent servant, one who kept turning back. Said of Ayyub, and it is the whole verdict on a life of that much loss.
I am better than him. You created me from fire and created him from clay. The first argument from pedigree, already heard in Makkan mouths earlier in the surah.

connections.why: Al-Anbiya passes Dawud, Sulayman and Ayyub in a few verses each. Sad slows the same three men down and adds what had gone wrong.
Al-A'raf gives the fullest account of the refusal of Iblis and what followed, where Sad gives the argument he made and stops.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Sad. What is authentically established is a practice rather than a reward: Ibn Abbas said that Sad is not among the definitive prostrations of the Qur'an, and that he nevertheless saw the Prophet ﷺ prostrate at it, recorded by Bukhari in the book on the prostrations of the Qur'an.
