The schools differ over whether that prostration is one of recitation or one of thanks.
virtue.src: no virtue report; the prostration at 38:24 reported from Ibn Abbas in Bukhari, book of the prostrations of the Qur'an

context: Ghafir is Makkan and opens the run of seven consecutive surahs beginning with the letters Ha Mim. It belongs to the later Makkan years, when believers were being held and worn down for what they had said out loud, and it spends most of its length on one parallel: Musa sent to Fir'awn, and a man inside Fir'awn's household who was a believer in secret.

That parallel explains the construction. The surah opens with four descriptions of Allah stacked into a single verse, forgiving of sin, accepting repentance, severe in penalty, owner of abundance, and then spends eighty verses showing people meeting one side of that or the other.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from verse three, which calls Allah Ghafir adh-dhanb, the Forgiver of sin, first of four descriptions stacked in that verse. The surah's other and older name is Al-Mu'min, the Believer, after the man of Fir'awn's household who concealed his faith. Both names fit, and they pull in different directions.

movements.note: Revelation from the Exalted in Might, the Knowing, described as Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, severe in penalty, owner of abundance. Then the angels carrying the Throne, asking forgiveness for the believers and their families.
The regret of those who denied, the Day of the Approaching Event when hearts are at the throats, and the statement that Allah is swift in account. Peoples before them were greater in strength.

movements.h: The man who had said nothing
movements.note: Musa sent with signs to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun, and the order to kill the sons of the believers. A man of Fir'awn's family who had hidden his faith asks why they would kill a man for saying my Lord is Allah.

The weak and the arrogant blaming one another inside the punishment, and their request that the keepers of Hell ask for one day's relief, which comes back refused. Then the command: call upon Me, I will respond.

movements.h: Night, day, and the shape you were given
movements.note: Allah who made the night for rest and the day for seeing, the earth a place of settlement and the sky a structure, and who formed you and perfected your forms. The instruction follows to call on the Ever-Living.

Those who dispute the verses of Allah are dragged in shackles, and messengers are mentioned whose accounts were never told. The surah closes on people who believed only once they had seen the punishment.

themes.t: The angels ask for people they never met
themes.d: Those who carry the Throne ask forgiveness for the believers, then ask that their parents, spouses and offspring be admitted with them. A curtain lifts for three verses, and behind it is a prayer about people who cannot hear it.
Call upon Me, I will respond to you. The sentence immediately after names refusal to ask as arrogance, which moves supplication out of the category of optional acts.
The phrase returns through the whole surah, and each time the motive is named rather than the argument answered: in their breasts is nothing but pride, which they will never reach.
The man of Fir'awn's household concealed his faith for years and is quoted at length exactly once, when the killing of Musa is discussed. Nothing is said of what became of him.

heart: Recited slowly, the third verse is the one to sit with, because it will not let a reader keep one half of Allah without the other. Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, severe in penalty, owner of abundance. Four descriptions, one verse, nothing softening the join.

The speech of the believing man changes on a slow reading too, mostly because of how it ends. He has argued, warned and reminded them of Yusuf, and got nowhere. His last words are not a threat. You will remember what I say to you, and I entrust my affair to Allah.

passages.why: Forgiver of sin, Accepter of repentance, severe in penalty, owner of abundance. Both halves arrive in one breath, which is how the surah means them to be held.
The bearers of the Throne asking forgiveness for those who believed, and for their fathers, spouses and descendants. A prayer said about people who cannot hear it.
Would you kill a man because he says my Lord is Allah, while he has brought you clear proofs. Spoken inside the room where the killing was planned.
Call upon Me, I will respond to you. A command before it is a promise, and the sentence after says what declining to ask amounts to.

connections.why: Al-Qasas tells Musa's years in Egypt at length, including the man who ran from the far end of the city to warn him. Ghafir shows that court from inside.
Fussilat is the next Ha Mim surah and picks up where this one leaves off, moving from those who dispute the signs to the signs themselves.

virtue.text: No authentic prophetic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Ghafir. What is reported is a companion's remark: Ibn Mas'ud is quoted as calling the Ha Mim surahs the brocade of the Qur'an. That is his own assessment and not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ, so it carries a companion's weight and nothing beyond it. The surah's standing rests instead on its opening verse and on the speech of the believer of Fir'awn's family.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; Ibn Mas'ud's remark on the Ha Mim surahs

context: Fussilat is Makkan and the second of the Ha Mim surahs. The biographies record a widely told occasion for its opening: Utbah ibn Rabi'ah of Quraysh came to the Prophet ﷺ with an offer of wealth and authority if he would stop. The Prophet ﷺ recited this surah to him, and at the verse warning of a thunderbolt like that of 'Ad and Thamud, Utbah put his hand over his mouth. The account comes from the biographies, not the hadith collections.

The surah's shape matches that scene. It addresses people who had decided in advance not to listen, and quotes them saying so: our hearts are in coverings, in our ears is deafness, and between us and you is a partition. Against a refusal that specific, the surah offers detail rather than spectacle.
surahs.name_story: Fussilat comes from the third verse: a Book whose verses have been set out in detail, an Arabic Qur'an for a people who know. The word means distinguished clause by clause. The surah is also called Ha Mim as-Sajdah, after its opening letters and the prostration in it, and the first name states its answer to the demand for a sign.

movements.h: A Book set out in detail
movements.note: The revelation described as detailed and Arabic, and the refusal of most who hear it. They say their hearts are covered and their ears deaf, and the reply is that the man bringing it is a human like them.

The making of the earth and its provision, then the heaven which was smoke and was told to come willingly or unwillingly and answered that it comes willingly. The passage ends on the Day a person's hearing, sight and skin testify against him.

movements.h: Say our Lord is Allah, then hold
movements.note: The plan to speak over the recitation and drown it out, then the promise to those who say our Lord is Allah and remain straight: angels descending with do not fear and do not grieve.

movements.h: The sun and the moon are not the point
movements.note: Among His signs are the night and the day and the sun and the moon, with the instruction not to prostrate to the sun or the moon but to the One who created them. The prostration falls here, and the schools differ over whether it belongs at verse thirty seven or verse thirty eight.

Deeds returning to whoever did them, and the human habit of never tiring of asking for good while despairing when harm arrives. The surah closes with the promise of signs shown in the horizons and within themselves.

themes.d: The standing demand in Makkah was for a sign, and this surah's name announces a different reply. Verse forty four adds that a foreign recitation would have been objected to just as loudly.
Those who said our Lord is Allah and then remained on a right course. The condition attached to the promise of descending angels is not the statement but what follows it.
Repel by that which is better, and the enemy becomes as a devoted friend. The next verse says at once that this is granted only to the patient.
The hearing, the sight and the skins testify, and the reason given is an assumption rather than an appetite: they thought Allah did not know much of what they did.

heart: Recited slowly, the pair of verses at thirty four and thirty five is the hardest thing in this surah, because it addresses somebody who has been wronged and is within their rights. Repel by that which is better, and the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as a devoted friend.

The ending places the evidence in two locations at once. We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear that it is the truth. The second half turns a reader back on themselves, which for a surah answering people who arranged not to listen is the right last move.

passages.why: Those who said our Lord is Allah and then remained on a right course, the angels descend upon them: do not fear and do not grieve. Two instructions covering most of what troubles a person.
Who is better in speech than one who invites to Allah and does righteousness and says, indeed I am of the Muslims. The order of the clauses is worth noticing.
Repel by that which is better, with the qualification arriving immediately: only the patient are granted it, and only one given a great share.
We will show them Our signs in the horizons and within themselves until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.

connections.why: Ghafir is the Ha Mim before it and returns repeatedly to those who dispute the signs. Fussilat describes the Book those signs are set out in.
Al-Furqan records the complaint that his people took this Qur'an as a thing abandoned. Fussilat records one method: speak over it so nobody can hear.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Fussilat. The account most often attached to it is the story of Utbah ibn Rabi'ah, a report about one man's reaction on one afternoon, preserved in the biographies rather than the hadith collections and promising nothing to anyone who reads the surah. What it rests on is its own claim, that a Book set out in detail is the sign they wanted.
virtue.src: no authentic virtue report

context: Ash-Shura is Makkan and belongs to the Ha Mim group, though it is the only surah in the Qur'an opening with two separate sets of disconnected letters, Ha Mim followed by 'Ayn Sin Qaf. It was revealed to a community with no state, no army and no voice in how Makkah was governed, and the verse that names it describes believers as people whose affairs are settled by consultation.

The gap between that description and those circumstances matters. Consultation appears here not as a constitutional arrangement but as a trait of a certain kind of person, listed between establishing prayer and spending. Injury is handled the same way. The surah grants the wronged the right to answer back, then rates pardon higher without withdrawing it.
surahs.name_story: The name is taken from a single word in verse thirty eight, wa amruhum shura baynahum, and their affair is consultation among themselves. Nothing else in the surah concerns consultation. Naming a whole surah from one word inside a list of qualities indicates the weight the tradition placed on it, and it fixes where the word belongs.

movements.h: Two sets of letters, and nothing like Him
movements.note: Revelation given to this Prophet ﷺ as it was given to those before him, and the heavens almost splitting from above while the angels ask forgiveness for those on earth. The passage states that there is nothing like unto Him.

What was enjoined on Nuh, revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, and enjoined on Ibrahim, Musa and 'Isa, summarised in two instructions: establish the religion and do not divide over it. Division is traced to a point after knowledge arrived.

Whoever wants the harvest of the Hereafter has it increased, while whoever wants this world alone gets some of it and no share in the other. The surah then says no payment is asked except affection for the near of kin, a phrase read variously: Ibn Abbas is recorded in Bukhari explaining it as the kinship between the Prophet ﷺ and the clans of Quraysh, and others read it as love for his household.

movements.h: What hands earned, and what to do next
movements.note: Whatever strikes you of disaster comes from what your own hands earned, and He pardons much. Then the description of the believers, consultation included, and the passage on answering injury: retaliation in kind is permitted, and pardon carries a reward with Allah.

The wrongdoers asking whether there is any way back, and the giving of daughters to whom He wills and sons to whom He wills. The surah closes by stating that Allah speaks to a human being only through revelation, from behind a veil, or by sending a messenger.

themes.d: The word shura appears once, inside a list of what believers are like, with no procedure attached. Scholars have long differed over whether the outcome of a consultation binds the one who called it.

There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing. Resemblance is denied and attributes affirmed in one sentence, which is why the verse anchors nearly every discussion of the divine descriptions.

themes.t: The right kept, the better named
themes.d: The recompense for an evil act is an evil one like it. The permission is real and is never taken back, and the verse then says whoever pardons and sets matters right has his reward with Allah.
Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa and Muhammad ﷺ received the same instruction, stated in two parts: establish the religion, and do not divide over it. The second part carries as much weight as the first.

heart: Recited slowly, verse thirty will unsettle a reader who has been treating hardship as an accident. Whatever strikes you of disaster is from what your own hands have earned. What keeps the line from crushing is the clause attached to it, easy to pass over: and He pardons much.

The surah's other slow verse is its shortest theological sentence. There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing. It does two opposite things at once, closing off every comparison a mind reaches for and then leaving two attributes standing.

passages.why: There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the Hearing, the Seeing. The verse every discussion of the divine attributes returns to, in every century.
The same religion enjoined on Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa and 'Isa and revealed to Muhammad ﷺ, stated as establish it and do not divide in it.
Whatever strikes you of disaster is from what your hands have earned, and He pardons much. The second half is usually the half that gets dropped.
And their affair is consultation among themselves. One clause inside a list of qualities, and a whole surah takes its name from it.

connections.why: Al 'Imran carries the command to the Prophet ﷺ to consult them in the matter, given in Madinah after a battle went badly. Ash-Shura describes the habit years earlier.
Fussilat is the Ha Mim before it and concerns how the Book was set out. Ash-Shura closes on how revelation reaches a human being at all.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Ash-Shura. Its distinction is textual rather than devotional: it is the only surah opening with two separate sets of disconnected letters, and it carries verse eleven, the sentence cited more than any other in discussions of how Allah is to be described.
virtue.src: no authentic virtue report

context: Az-Zukhruf is Makkan, from the years when the opposition had stopped disputing whether God exists and started disputing who should carry His message. Verse 31 preserves their exact objection: this Qur'an should have come down on a great man from one of the two cities, meaning Makkah or Ta'if. The surah answers a society that read worth off property and standing, and it answers on that ground rather than changing the subject.

That setting explains why so much of the surah is furniture. Ceilings of silver, stairways, doors, couches, gold ornament, bracelets, plates and cups: the vocabulary keeps returning until a reader notices that the Makkan objection and Pharaoh's objection to Musa run on one logic. A man who matters will be decorated. The reply is not that wealth is evil, but that it is handed out, and by someone else.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from verse 35, where gold ornament closes a list of what the houses of the deniers could have been given. What makes the list bite is the reason attached to it: these things are withheld only because people would otherwise rush as one community into the same error, not because they are too valuable to give. Naming the surah after the ornament keeps that argument in front of the reader for eighty-nine verses.

movements.h: An Arabic Qur'an, and what they concede
movements.note: The oath by the clear Book, the statement that it is with Allah in the Mother of the Book, then a run of things the deniers admit when asked: the earth made a bed, water sent down in measure, cattle and ships made to ride. It closes with the words to say on mounting.

movements.h: Daughters for Allah, fathers for themselves
movements.note: They assign daughters to Allah while the face of one of them darkens at the birth of a girl. Pressed for a reason, they produce only the practice of their fathers, and the surah notes that the affluent of every town gave their warner that same sentence.

movements.h: Ibrahim's word, and the ornament withheld
movements.note: Ibrahim's disavowal of his father's worship is called a word left among his descendants. Against it stands the demand that revelation arrive with a great man, answered by the reminder that livelihood itself is apportioned, and by the passage on silver ceilings and gold. Whoever turns from the remembrance is assigned a devil for company.

Musa comes with signs and Pharaoh replies by pointing at the kingdom of Egypt and the rivers running beneath him, then asks why no gold bracelets were thrown to Musa. He made light of his people, they obeyed, and the drowning follows.

movements.h: The son of Maryam as a taunt
movements.note: Isa is raised in argument and the gathering laughs aloud. He was a servant favoured, the surah answers, and it turns to the Hour, where close friends become enemies except for those who feared Allah.

movements.h: Malik, and the order to withdraw
movements.note: From the Fire the criminals call to Malik for an end and are told they will remain. The claim of a son is refused outright, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to leave them to their talk, turn aside, and say peace.

themes.d: Both Quraysh and Pharaoh treat decoration as proof of standing: a great man should have received the Book, a true messenger should have arrived in gold. The surah never says they are wrong about gold. It says the One distributing the gold is the One distributing prophethood.

The single reason the deniers offer for their worship is what they found their fathers doing, and the surah reports it from three different mouths. What is being examined is not a bad argument but the absence of one.
Verse 32 puts provision in Allah's hands and says ranks exist so that people may put one another to use. A source of pride is thereby turned into an arrangement nobody selected for himself.

A man turned away from the remembrance is given a companion who stays with him to the reckoning, where he wishes for the distance of the two easts between them. Company is treated here as a consequence rather than an accident.

heart: Recited without hurry, Az-Zukhruf works on a reader's sense of what a serious life looks like. Its lists are all household goods, and none of them is condemned. The gold that verse 35 calls the enjoyment of this life is circulating on plates in verse 71, inside the Garden. What changes between the two verses is not the metal but who is holding it and when.

The other thing the surah keeps in view is speech: what people say when asked why they believe what they believe. Their answer does not change across generations or across towns. Attentive recitation tends to send a reader back to his own reasons, which is uncomfortable and is the point. It ends by telling the Prophet ﷺ to say peace and step back, which is also what it leaves a reader holding: an argument he no longer has to win in the room.

passages.why: The words the Prophet ﷺ said on mounting a ride, taken from the surah itself. They turn an ordinary departure into an admission of who made the animal carry a man and where the road ends.

The answer to anyone who reads his own standing as self-made. Provision is apportioned, ranks exist so people can use one another's work, and the mercy of the Lord is worth more than what they gather.
The verses that give the surah its name. Silver ceilings would cost nothing to grant, which is what makes the passage difficult for anyone who reads wealth as approval.
Friendships built on anything other than fear of Allah are shown coming apart on the Day itself. Short enough to memorise and easy to test against one's own attachments.

connections.why: Saba' records the affluent of every town meeting their warner with their wealth and children, in nearly the words Quraysh use here. Read together, they show the objection was never local to Makkah.
Al-Kahf's man with two gardens says what these opponents say, at the length of a story rather than a slogan, and receives the same verdict on what the adornment of this life is worth.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Az-Zukhruf. What is established in the Sunnah is narrower and more usable: Sahih Muslim records that the Prophet ﷺ said the words of verses 13 and 14 when he settled onto a mount, so those two verses have a fixed place in practice while the surah as a whole carries no promised reward. Its standing rests on its argument and on its place among the seven surahs that open with Ha Mim.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; the words said on mounting, in Sahih Muslim

context: Ad-Dukhan is Makkan and short, and it addresses people who had heard the message and treated it as entertainment. It opens on the night the Qur'an came down and closes by telling the Prophet ﷺ to watch, since they are watching too. Between those points it sets one warning beside another with almost no connective argument.

Its central image, a smoke covering the people, was read two ways by the earliest authorities and still is. Ibn Mas'ud held that it had already come, in the famine that struck Quraysh so hard that a hungry man looking up saw something like smoke between himself and the sky, and his explanation is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari. Others read it as a sign still ahead, and a report in Sahih Muslim lists a smoke among the signs preceding the Hour. The matter is disputed, and the surah does not settle it.
surahs.name_story: Named from verse 10, where the sky is told to bring a visible smoke that covers the people. The word occurs once and the surah is named for it, which is a fair guide to how the surah operates: one image, held long enough that what follows it becomes the real subject. Under the smoke people say plainly that they believe, and the answer given is that a clear messenger had already reached them.

movements.h: The night the Book came down
movements.note: An oath by the clear Book, then the statement that it was sent down on a blessed night in which every wise matter is made distinct. The passage grounds the revelation in mercy from a Lord who gives life and takes it.

movements.h: Smoke, and a promise made under it
movements.note: The deniers are left in their amusement and told to watch for a sky bearing visible smoke. They will ask for the torment to be lifted and will declare themselves believers. The lifting is described as brief, and a greater seizure is named after it.

movements.h: Pharaoh, and a sea left as it was
movements.note: Musa asks that the servants of Allah be handed over, then is told to travel by night and to leave the sea as it was, because the army behind him is to be drowned. What that court left behind of gardens, springs, crops and pleasant places is inventoried, and the surah says heaven and earth did not weep for them.

Quraysh demand their ancestors be produced as proof of resurrection. They are asked whether they are better than the people of Tubba', a title borne by kings in Yemen, and told that the heavens and the earth were not created in play.
Zaqqum is described as the food of the sinful, boiling in bellies like scalding water. The man being dragged is addressed with the very titles of honour he once claimed for himself.

movements.h: A secure place, and one death only
movements.note: Those who feared Allah are placed in gardens and springs, in fine silk, tasting no death beyond the first. The surah ends by saying the Qur'an has been made easy on the Prophet's ﷺ tongue, and telling him to watch.

themes.d: The plea under the smoke is a complete profession of belief, and it is refused, because a clear messenger had already come and been dismissed. This surah measures belief by when it arrives, not by how it is worded.

Revelation descends on a night in which every wise matter is made distinct. Most commentators identify it as the Night of Decree in Ramadan, in line with the statement elsewhere that the Qur'an was sent down in Ramadan; a minority among the early authorities placed it in mid-Sha'ban, and the majority did not accept that.
Verse 29 is among the coldest lines in the Qur'an. A regime holding gardens, springs and noble estates is removed, and the only comment offered is that the sky and the earth did not weep for them.

The demand to watch a resurrection happen now is met with the purpose of creation instead of a demonstration. If the heavens and earth were not made as amusement, a day of settled accounts is not an extra claim but the thing that makes the rest hold together.

heart: Ad-Dukhan can be recited in a single sitting, and its pace is what a reader notices first. It moves without transition from a night of decree to a smoke, from a drowning to a tree, from the tree to silk and springs. Nothing is developed or explained. Taking it slowly leaves each image standing on its own, which is how it was built.

Most readers stop at the plea made under the smoke, because it is the prayer anyone would make and it comes too late to count. Reciting that verse with attention raises a plain question about the timing of one's own return, and the surah does not soften it. What it does instead is end on the far side, in a place of safety where the only death ever tasted is the one already behind.

passages.why: The descent of the Qur'an is placed on a blessed night in which every wise matter is separated out. Read with the statement that the Qur'an was sent down in Ramadan, this is the ground of what is sought in the last ten nights.
The words of people asking for the torment to be lifted and promising belief. Worth pausing on because the wording of the plea is faultless and it changes nothing.
Heaven and earth did not weep for them. One sentence measures what a power that ruled a whole country was actually worth.
The reply to a demand for resurrection on request. Creation was not play, and this is one of the most compact statements of that argument anywhere in the Qur'an.

connections.why: Al-Qadr names the night that Ad-Dukhan describes and adds what descends on it. Commentators read each in the light of the other, and neither is complete alone.
Ash-Shu'ara gives the exchange between Musa and Pharaoh at length. Ad-Dukhan compresses it to a dozen verses and keeps the ending, so reading them in sequence shows what the compression is for.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Ad-Dukhan. A report does circulate about reciting it on the night before Friday, with forgiveness promised or angels seeking forgiveness for the reciter; it is found in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, who called it gharib himself, and later hadith critics graded it weak. It is not relied on here. The authentic material touching this surah concerns what the smoke refers to, which is a question of meaning and not a reward for recitation.
virtue.src: no authentic prophetic virtue report; the Friday-night report in Jami' at-Tirmidhi is graded weak

context: Al-Jathiyah is Makkan and sits inside the run of surahs opening with Ha Mim. Its audience had settled on a position and stated it in a sentence: this life is all there is, we die and we live, and nothing finishes a man except the passing of time. Verse 24 quotes them saying exactly that.

The structure follows from the position. The surah does not open with the Hereafter, it opens with what those same people looked at daily: the sky and the earth, their own making, the animals spread across the ground, night giving way to day, rain reviving dead land, the turning of the winds. Each is called a sign, and each is addressed to a differently named audience, those who believe, those who are certain, those who reason, those who reflect. The argument is that evidence was never in short supply.
surahs.name_story: The name is taken from verse 28, where every nation is seen kneeling and called to its own record. The Arabic word describes people down on their knees, the posture of someone waiting on a verdict rather than someone praying. A surah that begins by quoting men who say only time destroys them is named for the moment those same men are on their knees while the record is read out.

movements.note: Heavens and earth, the creation of the reader himself, the creatures scattered over the ground, night and day, rain and wind. Set against all of it is the man who hears the verses recited and then persists in arrogance as though he never heard a word.

The sea is made to carry ships, and whatever is in the heavens and the earth is placed at people's disposal, all of it from Him. A hard instruction follows: tell the believers to forgive those who have no expectation of the days of Allah.

movements.h: Israel, and a road of your own
movements.note: The Children of Israel were given scripture, judgement, prophethood and clear proofs, and then differed out of rivalry once knowledge had reached them. The Prophet ﷺ is placed on a clear road and told to follow it rather than the inclinations of people who do not know.

Those who pile up evil are told they will not be handled like the believers. The man who takes his own desire as his god is described with hearing sealed and sight veiled, and the deniers are quoted saying that nothing destroys them but time.

The Hour arrives, each community is called to a record that speaks against it in truth, and the record turns out to have been transcribed while the deeds were being done. All greatness in the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, and the surah stops there.

themes.d: Naming dahr as the thing that kills men puts an impersonal process where a Lord belongs. The Qur'an answers by naming the One who gives life and takes it, and the same substitution is still made today in newer vocabulary.

themes.t: The signs are graded by the one looking
themes.d: The same sky is called a sign for those who reason, for those who are certain, for those who reflect, and for those who believe. The difference is located in the observer, not in the object.

Verse 23 does not describe an idol of stone or an inherited cult. It describes a man whose god is what he wants, and it treats the deafness that follows as the result of a choice rather than a defect he was born with.
The register is not compiled at the end from memory. Verse 29 says it was being transcribed as the deeds were done, which makes the Day a reading rather than an investigation.

heart: This is a short surah with a very fast descent. Eleven verses carry a reader from the sky above his head to a man who hears the words of Allah and keeps walking, and twenty more reach an entire nation on its knees. Recited without hurry, that pace is what does the work, since nothing in it is repeated for emphasis.

The verse people tend to carry away is the one about a man whose god is his own desire, because it does not describe a foreign practice. Its wording lets a reader notice how a preference hardens into a principle and then into a rule nobody is allowed to question. Set against it stands the instruction in verse 14 to forgive those who expect nothing from the days of Allah, which keeps the surah from becoming a complaint about other people.

passages.why: Believers are told to forgive those who have no expectation of the days of Allah. Commentators differ over whether this was later superseded by the verses on fighting or stands as guidance on absorbing insult, and the disagreement is old and unresolved.
The only place in the Qur'an where the word shari'ah occurs. It is used of a road laid out to be walked, and it is set directly against following the inclinations of those who do not know.

The god made of desire, and the claim that time is what destroys men. A hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim forbids abusing time and gives the reason: the alternation of night and day is Allah's own doing.
Every nation kneeling, and a record that speaks in truth because it was written down as the deeds happened. This is the image the surah is named for.

connections.why: Al-Furqan carries almost the same sentence about the man who takes his desire as his god, and follows it with a question about who could possibly be made responsible for such a person. The two verses are best read side by side.

Al-Insan opens by asking whether a stretch of time passed over man when he was not a thing worth mentioning. Al-Jathiyah's deniers say time is what destroys them; the other surah reminds them that time is also what they came out of.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Jathiyah. The long lists that assign a named reward to every surah in order, most of them going back to a narration attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, are judged forged by hadith critics, and nothing from that material is used here. This surah's standing rests on its content, and it is worth noting that a hadith qudsi in Bukhari and Muslim takes up its subject directly by forbidding the abuse of time.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; the fabricated series attributed to Ubayy ibn Ka'b is excluded

context: Al-Ahqaf is Makkan and comes last of the seven surahs that open with Ha Mim. Commentators place it late in the Makkan period, when the arguments had been made and refused and the pressure on the Prophet ﷺ was to hold a position rather than to win one. Its final instruction is to be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient.

Two things in it fit that setting. The passage on the jinn who stopped to listen and went home to their people as warners is commonly placed by the commentators on the return from Ta'if, when the Prophet ﷺ had been driven out of a town and had no human audience left, though reports differ over the details. And the destruction of 'Aad is told through their own mistake: they watched a cloud move toward their valleys and were pleased by it, because they took it for rain.
surahs.name_story: Al-Ahqaf is a place name, the long curving sand dunes where 'Aad lived, and it occurs once, in verse 21, where Hud is described warning his people there. The surah takes its title from a landscape rather than a doctrine or an argument. That fits what is left of 'Aad by the end of the account: dwellings standing in sand, with nothing else in view.

movements.note: Creation is stated to be in truth and for a fixed term. A challenge follows for those who call on others besides Allah: point to a piece of the earth they created, or produce a book from before this, or any remnant of transmitted knowledge.

movements.h: Not a novelty among the messengers
movements.note: The charge that the Qur'an was invented is met with the Prophet's ﷺ own limits: he is not the first of the messengers and does not know what will be done with him. A witness from the Children of Israel is mentioned, and those who say our Lord is Allah and then hold straight are told no fear will come upon them.

A man is enjoined to treat his parents well: his mother carried him with hardship, and thirty months cover his bearing and weaning. At forty he asks to be made grateful and to have his children set right. Beside him stands a son who says uff to his parents and denies he will ever be raised.

Hud warns his people and is told to bring on what he threatens. Seeing a cloud head for their valleys, they welcome it as rain. It is a wind, and afterwards nothing can be seen but their dwellings, though they had been given hearing, sight and hearts.

A company of jinn turns aside to hear the Qur'an, tells one another to keep quiet, and goes back to its people as warners. The surah closes on the power that made the heavens and the earth and on the order to endure as the resolute messengers endured.

themes.d: The demand in verse 4 is for a scripture or a remnant of knowledge, meaning a trace of something actually transmitted. A claim about God is treated as the kind of claim that has to come from somewhere and can be asked for.

Verse 9 has the Prophet ﷺ say that he does not know what will be done with him or with them. A claim to prophecy is kept separate here from a claim to independent knowledge of the unseen, and the surah keeps the two apart deliberately.

The du'a at forty is spoken by a man whose parents are now old and whose children are watching. Placing it next to the son who says uff shows the surah's interest: the same upbringing can produce either, and the difference surfaces in what each one says about being raised again.

'Aad saw the cloud and were pleased. The failure was not disbelief in that instant but a settled habit of reading whatever arrives as approval, which is also said of those who used up their good things in this life.

heart: Al-Ahqaf is a surah about correct hearing. A company of jinn catch a recitation by accident and immediately tell one another to be silent. 'Aad were given hearing and sight and hearts, and verse 26 states that none of it availed them anything. Between those two pictures the surah asks nothing of a reader except that he work out which one describes his own attention.

The verse most people take away is verse 15, and it repays being said slowly, because it holds a whole life in one sentence: hardship in carrying, hardship in delivery, thirty months, then forty years, then a request to be made grateful for what was spent on him and to have the same continue in his children. It is a du'a made by someone old enough to have added it up.

passages.why: The Prophet ﷺ is made to say that he is not the first of the messengers and does not know what will be done with him. A whole category of claims about him is ruled out here in his own words.
Those who say our Lord is Allah and then hold straight. A statement and a course of conduct, and the surah rests the entire promise of security on the pair of them together.

The verse on parents, the thirty months of bearing and weaning, and the du'a at forty. Jurists read it alongside the two years of nursing named in Al-Baqarah to derive a minimum term of pregnancy of six months.

The order to be patient as the messengers of firm resolve were patient. Commentators differ over who is meant, most naming a small group of the greatest messengers and some taking the phrase to include them all.

connections.why: Al-Jinn reports the same night from the other side and at greater length, in the listeners' own words. Al-Ahqaf keeps only what they did afterwards, which is the part its argument needs.
Al-Haqqah describes the end of 'Aad in detail, a wind loosed on them for seven nights and eight days. Al-Ahqaf gives the hour before that, while they were still watching the cloud and expecting rain.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Ahqaf. Its standing rests on its content, and on the fact that the episode in verses 29 to 32 is not an isolated tale: an account of the jinn hearing the Prophet's ﷺ recitation is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim on the authority of Ibn Abbas. That report establishes the event itself. It does not attach any reward to reciting the surah, and nothing authentic does.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; Ibn Abbas's account of the jinn in Bukhari and Muslim

context: Surah Muhammad is Medinan, and most commentators place it in the first years after the Hijrah, around the time of Badr, though no authentic report fixes the date. It carries a second and older name, Al-Qital, the surah of fighting, and that name describes its subject more exactly. Verse 13 speaks of the town that drove the Prophet ﷺ out, which commentators connect to the departure from Makkah itself.

The setting explains the split screen. Nearly every passage runs two columns at once: those who disbelieve and block the road, and those who believe and act rightly; deeds sent astray, and deeds set right. It also explains the second subject, which is not the enemy outside the city but the men inside it who found a revelation about fighting hard to hear, and who are described watching the Prophet ﷺ with the stare of a man fainting at death.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from verse 2, one of four places in the Qur'an where the Prophet ﷺ is called Muhammad. The verse sets his name inside a condition: those who believe in what was sent down upon Muhammad, and it is the truth from their Lord, have their misdeeds removed and their state repaired. The naming is not decorative. It marks the point at which belief is tied to a particular man and a particular revelation rather than to general piety.

movements.note: The deeds of those who block the way of Allah are sent astray, while the misdeeds of the believers are removed from them. The rule of engagement follows, along with the two dispositions named for captives once the war lays down its burdens: release as a favour, or ransom.

movements.h: If you help Him, He helps you
movements.note: Support given to Allah is answered with support and with feet made firm. Towns stronger than Makkah are recalled and their remains offered as evidence. The stretch ends with rivers of water, milk, wine and honey set against water that scalds the bowels.

Some sit and listen to the Prophet ﷺ, then step outside and ask those given knowledge what he had said just now. Guidance is described as increasing for the guided, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to know that there is no god but Allah and to seek forgiveness.

movements.h: A surah they did not want
movements.note: The believers ask why no surah has come down, and when one comes down with fighting in it the sick of heart look on like men at the point of death. The passage warns about spreading corruption and cutting kinship, asks whether they ponder the Qur'an at all, and describes those who turned back after guidance was clear.

movements.h: Known by the way they talk
movements.note: Concealed hatred is said to surface in the bend of a man's speech, and testing is promised until the strivers and the patient are distinguished. Obedience is commanded and invalidating one's own deeds forbidden, and the surah closes on money: whoever withholds withholds from himself, and a people who turn away will be replaced.

themes.d: The language of works being made to fail runs the length of the surah, applied first to those who block the road, then to those who hate what Allah revealed, and finally in verse 33 to the believers, who are told not to invalidate their own deeds. The warning turns inward before the end.

themes.t: Captives and the limits of war
themes.d: Verse 4 names two dispositions after the fighting stops, favour and ransom. The schools of law differ over whether other options remain open to a ruler and over how this verse stands in relation to later ones, and that disagreement is a matter for jurists, not for a study note.

Hypocrisy is detected here by sound rather than by inquiry. The Prophet ﷺ is told he will know them by the bending of their words, which puts the evidence in something a person cannot fully manage or hide.
A surah about fighting ends on wealth. Asked for a portion, people hold back, and the surah observes that Allah has no need of it while they do, so that a stingy man is being stingy against himself.

heart: The surah is blunt and its sentences are short. Recited slowly, what stands out is how often it turns from the enemy to the listener. The men it describes are not in Makkah. They are sitting in the mosque, hearing the Qur'an, then walking out and asking someone else what was just said.

Verse 24 asks whether they ponder the Qur'an or whether there are locks upon hearts, and it sits in the middle of a surah about people who heard everything and kept none of it. That placement makes it difficult to recite quickly. Verse 19, which tells the Prophet ﷺ to know that there is no god but Allah and then to seek forgiveness for himself and for the believing men and women, sets the order the whole surah works in: knowledge first, then repentance, then everything else.

passages.why: Support of Allah is answered with support and with feet made firm. The condition is stated first and the promise second, which is the whole force of the verse.

Knowledge of tawhid is commanded, then forgiveness sought for oneself and for the believing men and women. Al-Bukhari headed a chapter of his Book of Knowledge with this verse to argue that knowledge comes before speech and action.
Do they not ponder the Qur'an, or are there locks upon hearts. It asks for something beyond recitation and names in the same breath what prevents it.
Those who withhold withhold only from themselves, since Allah is the one free of need. The last line warns that a people who turn away will be replaced by others who will not be like them.

connections.why: The two sit side by side and both name the Prophet ﷺ. This one commands fighting and warns against calling for peace from a position of strength; the next records the truce he concluded at Hudaybiyah. Commentators differ over how the two fit together, and reading them in order is where the question begins.
Al-Anfal handles the same material at greater length, including what was done with the captives of Badr. Between them they carry most of the Medinan instruction on the conduct of war.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Surah Muhammad. Its standing rests on its subject, which is a community at war and the condition of the hearts inside it, and on the fact that it is the Qur'an's most sustained treatment of hypocrisy in a fighting context. Where it legislates, on captives in verse 4 and on truce in verse 35, the schools of law differ, and those differences belong to jurists rather than to a study note.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report

context: Al-Fath is Medinan and came down on the road back to Madinah in the sixth year after the Hijrah, following the events at Hudaybiyah. The Prophet ﷺ had set out with roughly fourteen hundred companions to perform 'umrah, not to fight. Quraysh blocked the road, and after long negotiation a treaty was signed on terms many companions found bitter: no 'umrah that year, a return the following year, and a clause requiring that anyone reaching Madinah from Makkah without his guardian's permission be sent back.

That explains the surah's insistence on the word conquest. Nothing had been taken, no battle fought, and the pilgrims went home without entering Makkah. The surah opens by calling the episode a clear conquest and then spends itself showing what was gained: a pledge taken under a tree, hands held back on both sides inside the sacred precinct, believers in Makkah unknown to the army who would have been trampled, and a truce that made ordinary contact possible. The companions themselves understood the conquest to be Hudaybiyah rather than the later entry into Makkah, and al-Bukhari records Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib saying so.
surahs.name_story: Named from the first verse, where what happened is called a clear conquest. The word carries the sense of an opening as much as a capture, and the surah uses it three times, once for what has already been granted and twice for something near at hand. Calling a treaty that disappointed an army a conquest is the surah's opening argument, made before a single reason is given for it.

movements.h: A conquest, and what it settles
movements.note: The declaration, then forgiveness, the completion of favour, guidance and help. Tranquility is described as sent down into the hearts of the believers so that they would increase in faith, and the hypocrites and idolaters who thought ill of Allah are named.
The Prophet ﷺ is described as witness, bringer of good news and warner. Then the pledge itself: those who give their word to him are giving it to Allah, and the hand of Allah is above their hands.

Bedouins who did not come offer their property and families as an excuse and are told what they had actually assumed. They are warned of a call to face a people of great might, and the blind, the lame and the ill are exempted by name.
Allah states His pleasure with those who pledged under the tree and says He knew what was in their hearts. A near opening and much spoil are promised, which commentators identify with Khaybar.

Had the Makkans fought, they would have turned in flight. Instead both sides were held back inside Makkah, and the reason given is the believing men and women in the city whom the army could not identify. Against the zeal of ignorance, tranquility was sent down and the word of God-consciousness fastened on the believers.

The vision that started the expedition is confirmed as true, with entry into the Sacred Mosque in safety and heads shaved or shortened. The surah ends describing the Prophet ﷺ and those with him as they appear in the Torah and in the Gospel, likened to a shoot that puts out side growth and stands firm on its stem.

themes.t: A defeat that was not one
themes.d: The method of the surah is to rename the event and then earn the name. What the army saw was a return without 'umrah; what the surah sets out is a truce that stopped the killing, sorted the sincere from the rest, and opened the roads.

Tranquility appears three times, always as a thing sent down, on the believers at the pledge and on the Prophet ﷺ with them. It is presented as given from outside rather than produced by good news, which matters here, because the news was not good.
Verse 24 makes the withholding of hands, on both sides and inside Makkah, the deed of Allah. A fight that did not happen is treated as an outcome rather than as an absence of one.

themes.t: Who was actually in the city
themes.d: The reason given for the restraint is unnamed believing men and women inside Makkah who would have been trampled without anyone knowing. An entire military decision is explained by people the army could not pick out.

heart: Al-Fath is a surah about being told that what you lived as a loss was a gain. Recited slowly it does not argue with the feeling; it lists what was true underneath it, item by item, until the list outweighs the disappointment. Umar's objections on that day and his regret afterwards are both preserved in Sahih al-Bukhari, which is part of why the surah is read the way it is.

Its second half keeps returning to what people were carrying inside them: what the bedouins assumed, what was in the hearts of those who pledged, the zeal that filled the hearts of Quraysh, the tranquility sent down on the believers. Read attentively it becomes a surah about interior states being weighed while an external event runs its course. It ends with a plant putting out shoots, the only picture of growth in it, placed directly after everything that had looked like standing still.

passages.why: A treaty that satisfied nobody is called a clear conquest, and forgiveness, completed favour, guidance and help are attached to it. Sahih al-Bukhari records that when it came down the Prophet ﷺ said a surah had been revealed to him more beloved to him than everything the sun rises upon.

Tranquility sent into the hearts of the believers so they would increase in faith on top of their faith. It describes calm as something added rather than achieved, and it arrived at the worst hour of the expedition.

Allah's pleasure with those who pledged under the tree, together with the statement that He knew what was in their hearts. This verse is the basis for the name Bay'at ar-Ridwan, the pledge of good pleasure.

The description of the Prophet ﷺ and those with him: firm against the deniers, merciful among themselves, marked by prostration, likened to a crop that strengthens its own shoots until it stands on its stem. It is the last word of the surah, and it describes a community rather than a battle.

connections.why: An-Nasr marks the entry into Makkah that this surah promised, in three verses, and its instruction is praise and seeking forgiveness rather than triumph. Read after Al-Fath, it shows what the truce was for.

Al-Mumtahanah legislates for the believing women who came from Makkah after this treaty was signed, which is the Hudaybiyah clause worked out in practice. It takes up the situation of believers still inside the city, which Al-Fath mentions only as a reason for restraint.

virtue.text: This is one of the few surahs with an authentic prophetic report attached to it. Sahih al-Bukhari records that when Al-Fath came down on the return from Hudaybiyah, the Prophet ﷺ said that a surah had been revealed to him more beloved to him than everything on which the sun rises, and then recited its opening. Bukhari and Muslim also record that he recited this surah on his mount on the day Makkah was conquered, with a quavering repetition in his voice. Both establish the standing of the surah and his own recitation of it. Neither promises a set reward to a reciter, and no authentic report does.
virtue.src: Sahih al-Bukhari for the Prophet's ﷺ words when it was revealed; Bukhari and Muslim for his recitation of it on the day of the conquest

context: Al-Hujurat is Medinan and belongs to the later years, when Madinah had become the centre of a state and delegations were arriving from tribes across Arabia. The rooms it is named for are the small dwellings of the Prophet's ﷺ wives, built against the mosque wall, and some of the arrivals stood outside them and shouted for him.

Because the setting is a crowded city rather than a besieged minority, the surah's subject is speech: who speaks first, how loudly, and about whom. Five of its verses open by addressing the believers, each introducing a rule about the tongue or the ear, and verse 13 widens the address to all humanity.
surahs.name_story: The hujurat are the rooms in which the Prophet's ﷺ wives lived, adjoining the mosque in Madinah, and the name is taken from verse 4, where men call to him from behind them instead of waiting until he comes out. Naming a surah for a domestic detail fixes its scale: not doctrine, not warfare, but the noise a man makes at another man's door.

movements.note: Believers are told not to put themselves ahead of Allah and His Messenger, not to raise their voices above his, and not to call to him from outside his rooms.
A report brought by a corrupt person must be checked, in case a people is harmed in ignorance and the harm regretted afterwards.
Where two parties of believers fight, the rest must reconcile them and act against the aggressor until it returns to Allah's command. The rule rests on one sentence: the believers are but brothers.
Mockery, insult, nicknames, suspicion, spying and backbiting are prohibited in turn, the last of them given an image instead of an argument, since the backbiter eats his dead brother's flesh.
Descent is stated as a means of recognition and not a rank, and bedouins who announced that they believed are told to say instead that they had submitted.
Faith is defined by what it produces, belief that does not afterwards doubt and striving with wealth and self, and the surah ends by declining to accept Islam as a favour done to Allah.

themes.d: These prohibitions arrive in the same imperative form as the rulings on fighting and reconciliation, which places a rumour and a nickname among the things a Muslim answers for.
Verse 6 ties verification to a consequence, harming a people in ignorance and regretting it later. The obligation falls on whoever hears the report, not only whoever started it.

The statement that believers are brothers arrives inside instructions for what to do when they are fighting, so it generates duties for third parties. Jurists built the law of rebellion on verse 9 and differ over its conditions.
The closing passage separates the outward act of submission from faith settling in the heart. It does not deny the bedouins' Islam; it declines to let them assess their own standing.

heart: Recited slowly, Al-Hujurat is uncomfortable in a particular way, because almost everything it forbids is ordinary. Nobody sets out to backbite. The surah names small acts that people perform without deciding to, then attaches them to the same authority that governs prayer and fasting.

Repeated reading also slows a person at verse 13, which is quoted often and read quickly. It does not abolish lineage but gives it a function, recognition, so that what a person carries from family, colour or tribe stands as description and not as merit. The criterion put in its place is one no reader can measure in anyone else.

passages.why: The verse that makes verification a duty, naming both the kind of report that triggers the rule and the harm it prevents.
Suspicion, spying and backbiting in one verse, with the image of eating a dead brother's flesh placed where it cannot be argued with.
The one address to all humanity here, and read alongside verse 11 it explains why mocking a people was forbidden two verses earlier.
The difference between saying we have believed and saying we have submitted, useful when weighing one's own claim rather than another's.

connections.why: An-Nur legislates after a false report nearly tore Madinah apart, and Al-Hujurat states the rule that would have stopped it: the case and the principle.
Al-Munafiqun treats faith claimed by the tongue and absent from the heart in its dangerous form; Al-Hujurat treats the same gap when it is merely premature.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Al-Hujurat. What is authentically recorded is an occasion: Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, a companion with a loud voice, feared after verse 2 came down that his deeds had been nullified, and the Prophet ﷺ sent word that he was a man of Paradise. That report, in Bukhari and Muslim, concerns the revelation and not a reward for reading. The surah's standing rests on its content, the Qur'an's most concentrated body of rulings on speech.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; occasion for 49:2 in Bukhari and Muslim

context: Qaf is Makkan and argues one point, that the dead will be raised. Its audience had a settled objection, quoted in the third verse, that a man who has died and become dust is beyond any return. The surah answers with no miracle, pointing instead at what the objectors already accepted: a sky without a crack in it, mountains, layered palm trees, and rain falling on dead ground.

The Makkan setting shows in the compression. There is no legislation and no community to organise, the eight peoples of verses 12 to 14 are named without a story told of any of them, and what the surah spends its length on instead is the moment of death and what follows it.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for the letter Qaf, which stands alone as its first verse and is followed at once by an oath by the glorious Qur'an. The title explains nothing, which is worth noticing: the disconnected letters are recited rather than decoded, and the earliest authorities did not agree on their meaning, several declining to say.

movements.note: The objection to a warner from among themselves, and to being raised out of dust, is answered with what is visible: a sky without flaws, mountains and gardens, rain reviving dead land. That last case is named as the pattern of the emergence from the graves.
Eight peoples are listed in three verses, from the people of Nuh to the people of Tubba', with nothing said of them except that they denied.
Allah's knowledge of what the soul whispers is stated, two recording angels are seated at right and left, and death arrives with the words that this is what he had been avoiding.

movements.h: The court and the two destinations
movements.note: A driver and a witness bring each soul, and Hell is asked whether it is full and answers by asking for more. Paradise is brought near, and the last word said of it is that with Him there is still more.

The heavens and the earth were made in six days with no fatigue touching Him, and the Prophet ﷺ is told to be patient, to glorify at both ends of the day, and to remind, since he was not sent to compel.

themes.t: Argument from what is already accepted
themes.d: Every proof offered for the resurrection is drawn from something the audience did not dispute. Rain on dead ground is the closest case, and the surah says of it plainly that the emergence is like that.

The two recording angels are seated immediately after the statement that Allah knows what the soul whispers, which makes the record a witness produced for the man rather than information supplied to his Lord.
Verse 22 describes the change at death as the lifting of something that had been in the way. Nothing new is disclosed; it is the eyesight that alters.

themes.t: Whoever has a heart, or listens
themes.d: The condition attached to benefit in verse 37 is attention rather than intelligence or standing, which fits a surah the Prophet ﷺ read weekly from the pulpit.

heart: Qaf can be read in one sitting, and it keeps the reader at close range throughout. The jugular vein, the whisper of the soul, an angel on either side, the intoxication of death: none of it is at a distance, and the lens never widens for long. The effect of attentive reading is a narrowing, since nearly everything described either is happening to the reader already or will.

The Prophet ﷺ read this surah from the pulpit every Friday, and one woman of Madinah said she learned it only from hearing him say it there. It was not kept for funerals or nights of fear but chosen for the ordinary weekly gathering of people who had come in from their work.

passages.why: Allah's nearness to man in a single clause, quoted constantly and rarely read in its setting, a sentence about knowing what the soul whispers.
Death described as an intoxication that arrives carrying the truth, addressed with the words that this is what you were avoiding.
The statement that the Day informs no one of anything new. What changes is the eyesight and not the facts.
The verse naming the condition under which a reminder works, describing two ways of being present and ruling out reading with neither.

connections.why: The Prophet ﷺ recited Qaf and Al-Qamar together at both Eids, and their content fits the pairing: Qaf argues that the Hour is coming, Al-Qamar recounts what became of those who waited for further proof.
Al-Qiyamah takes up the same objection about scattered bones and answers it with the fingertips, making the identical argument in a sharper register.

virtue.text: An authentic prophetic practice is attached to this surah, though not a stated reward for reading it. Umm Hisham bint Haritha said she learned Qaf only from the tongue of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who recited it every Friday on the pulpit, which is in Sahih Muslim 873. Muslim also records from Abu Waqid al-Laythi that he recited Qaf and Al-Qamar at the two Eids. These reports establish where the surah was read and how regularly, not a merit for the reciter.
virtue.src: Muslim 873; Eid recitation from Abu Waqid al-Laythi in Muslim

context: Adh-Dhariyat is Makkan, and it settles its subject in the first six verses: what you are promised is true, and the recompense is going to occur. Everything after that is evidence, drawn from the sky and the earth, the nightly habits of the righteous, the guests who came to Ibrahim, and the wreckage left by four earlier nations.

What it leaves out marks it as Makkan: no law, no organising of a community, no address to hypocrites. What it supplies instead answers two questions a harassed minority would have been asking, when the Day of Recompense is, asked mockingly in verse 12, and where provision comes from, answered in verse 22 and again at the close.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from the first word of the first verse, adh-dhariyat, the winds that scatter dust. The four opening oaths are usually read as a sequence of winds, clouds, ships and angels, though the early commentators differed over which is meant by each. The surah is therefore named for something invisible whose effects are not.

movements.note: Four oaths in four short verses land on one statement, that the recompense will occur. Those who ask mockingly when that Day is are shown held over the Fire, told to taste what they were impatient for.

movements.h: The righteous, and where provision comes from
movements.note: The people of the gardens are described by their nights: they slept little, sought forgiveness before dawn, and kept a share of their wealth for the one who asked and the one too restrained to ask.

Guests arrive, a fattened calf is brought, and their hands do not reach for it. Ibrahim conceals his fear, they give news of a knowing son, his wife strikes her face and calls herself barren, and they go on to Lut's people.
Musa is sent to Fir'awn, who turns away and says magician or madman. 'Ad is given a barren wind, Thamud is seized by a thunderbolt, and the people of Nuh are dealt with in one verse.

Three statements about creation follow one another, each a clause long, ending with the note that everything was made in pairs. Then comes the imperative the surah has been moving toward, to flee to Allah.
Earlier peoples said of their messengers exactly what Quraysh said of the Prophet ﷺ, magician or madman, and the surah closes by naming why jinn and mankind were created.

themes.t: Provision is not the reader's to arrange
themes.d: Verse 22 and verse 58 place sustenance entirely on Allah's side, inside a surah about the Day of Recompense. Worry about income is set beside doubt about the Hereafter, not treated separately.

themes.t: The purpose stated once and plainly
themes.d: Verse 56 gives the reason jinn and mankind exist in a single sentence, and its placement carries part of the meaning, since it arrives after a surah's worth of material about food, guests, wealth and rain.

Ibrahim's conduct with the guests is reported as a sequence of actions: he slips away to his family, returns with a fattened calf, brings it near. No verse commends him, and the reporting is the commendation.

Verse 52 observes that every earlier people used the same two words about their messenger. Since they were separated by centuries and could not have arranged it, the charge becomes evidence about the accusers.

heart: This surah rewards being read once out of order and then in order. Verses 15 to 19 describe the righteous entirely through habits: how much of the night they slept, when they sought forgiveness, what they set aside for those who asked and for those who never did. Nothing is said of what they felt, which makes the passage unusually testable against a reader's own week.

The other place that changes on slow reading is the command in verse 50, to flee to Allah. Flight assumes something fled from, and the verse does not name it. Coming after the built sky and the spread earth, it leaves a reader to notice that the only refuge named is the One whose punishment is escaped.

passages.why: The righteous described by their nights and their giving, concrete enough to check a life against rather than admire.
Provision placed in the heaven alongside what has been promised, one short verse that reframes an anxiety most readers carry daily.
The single imperative the surah builds toward, worth returning to for what it leaves unstated about the direction of the danger.
The stated purpose of the creation of jinn and mankind, read in place at the end of a surah about rain and wealth, not as a slogan.

connections.why: Hud tells the visit to Ibrahim and the destruction of Lut's people at length, with the dialogue Adh-Dhariyat leaves out. The compressed version is easier to hold; the long one explains it.
Al-Mursalat also opens with oaths by winds and drives toward the recompense, but works by refrain: one opening device put to two uses.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting Adh-Dhariyat. Reports circulating in later works that assign a named reward to each surah in turn were judged fabricated by the hadith critics, and nothing sound has been established for this one. Its standing rests on its content, above all verse 56, among the most cited verses in the Qur'an on why human beings exist.
virtue.src: no authentic virtue report

context: At-Tur is Makkan and belongs to the stretch of that period when objections to the Prophet ﷺ had hardened into a short list of names: soothsayer, madman, poet, forger. Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who came to Madinah after Badr while still a mushrik, said he heard him reciting this surah in Maghrib, and that at verses 35 and 36 his heart was about to fly; the report is in Bukhari and Muslim.

That setting explains the second half, which does not argue so much as close exits. Beginning at verse 30, question after question opens with the same word, each proposing some account of where this message came from, each left standing as an absurdity.
surahs.name_story: At-Tur is the mountain, which most commentators identify as the mount where Musa was addressed. It is the first of five things sworn by in the opening verses, alongside a book inscribed on unrolled parchment, the frequented House, the raised ceiling and the swollen sea. The name places the revelation given to Muhammad ﷺ in the same sworn list as the site of the revelation given to Musa.

movements.note: The mount, the inscribed book, the frequented House, the raised ceiling and the swollen sea are sworn by in the first six verses, establishing a single sentence: the punishment of your Lord will occur, and nothing repels it.
The heaven sways and the mountains move, and the deniers who had been amusing themselves in idle talk are thrust into the Fire and told that patience and impatience have become the same thing.

The righteous eat and recline, their believing descendants are joined to them without anything deducted from anyone's deeds, and then they turn to one another and speak about the fear they used to live with among their families.

The charges of soothsaying, madness, poetry and forgery are met with a challenge to produce a statement like it. Then the questions come in a series: were they created out of nothing, did they create the heavens and the earth, do they hold the treasuries.
If a piece of the sky fell on them they would call it heaped clouds, so the Prophet ﷺ is told to leave them until they meet their Day, and is given three fixed times at which to praise his Lord.

themes.t: The oath list as an argument
themes.d: Of the five things sworn by, four are physical and permanent, and the written book is set among them. That is the claim being made before any argument starts.

themes.t: A Garden with the family in it
themes.d: Verse 21 joins believing descendants to those who came before them and states that nobody's deeds are reduced in order to do it, so what is described is a household restored rather than a solitary prize.

The run of questions from verse 30 to verse 43 does not demonstrate the Qur'an's truth directly. It names every alternative account of its origin and leaves each visibly unsayable, so the field is cleared rather than won.
The instruction at the end is patience, and the reason given is not that the opposition will stop. It is that the Prophet ﷺ is in Allah's eyes, which speaks to supervision rather than outcomes.

heart: Read slowly, the middle of this surah is the part that stays. The people of the Garden are shown talking, and what they talk about is what they used to be afraid of. Their speech opens with an admission that among their families they had been people who feared, and it closes with the statement that they used to call upon Him before.

The other effect comes from the questions, and it depends on hearing them in sequence rather than one at a time. Each is answerable in principle, and each answer would be worse than the last. By verse 43 a reader has been walked past every available position and shown that nobody holding one had examined it.

passages.why: Believing descendants joined to those who came before them, with the note that nobody's deeds are diminished to make it happen.
The speech of the people of the Garden about who they used to be. The last clause carries it: we used to call upon Him before.
The two questions reported to have shaken Jubayr ibn Mut'im while he was still a mushrik, short enough to hold in mind and hard to leave unanswered.
The command to be patient with its reason given: you are in Our eyes. Worth returning to when patience is required and nothing is moving.

connections.why: Al-Qalam opens by denying the same charge of madness and closes with the same instruction to wait for the decision of the Lord: two angles on one accusation.
Adh-Dhariyat ends by noting that every earlier people called its messenger a magician or a madman, and At-Tur takes that accusation apart term by term.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting At-Tur. What is authentically recorded is that the Prophet ﷺ recited it. Jubayr ibn Mut'im heard him read it in the Maghrib prayer, and Umm Salama, unwell during Hajj, was told to circle the House riding behind the people while he prayed beside it reciting by the Mount and a Book inscribed. Both are in Bukhari and record his practice rather than a reward.
virtue.src: no prophetic virtue report; recitation reports from Jubayr ibn Mut'im and Umm Salama in Bukhari

context: An-Najm is Makkan and answers one charge in particular, that the Prophet ﷺ was producing the Qur'an out of his own inclination. Its first answer is testimony rather than argument: your companion has not strayed and does not speak from desire, and what he brought is revelation. It then describes what he saw, twice, insisting each time on the accuracy of the seeing rather than its grandeur.

Since the charge concerned invention, the second half turns to invention of another kind. The three goddesses of Makkah are named and then reduced to words: they are names you have named, you and your fathers, with no authority sent down. That opposition sets the shape: revelation on one side, inherited naming on the other.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for the star of its first verse, sworn by as it descends. Commentators differed over what the star is, some reading a particular star and others reading the Qur'an itself as it came down in portions. Either reading suits a surah about something arriving from above and a man who reported it exactly.

movements.note: The Prophet ﷺ is defended in three clauses: not astray, not speaking from desire, only conveying revelation. The one of great power approaches to within two bow lengths, and a second sighting is placed at the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary.
Al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are named, and the argument against them is not that they are weak but that they are empty, names handed down by fathers.
Those who call the angels by female names are following conjecture, which avails nothing against truth, and the stretch ends by forbidding people to declare themselves pure.
A man who gave a little and then stopped is referred to the scrolls of Musa and of Ibrahim, which are quoted: no bearer bears another's burden, and man has nothing except what he strove for.
Short clauses assign to Allah what people assign elsewhere: laughter and weeping, death and life, the two mates from a drop, wealth and what suffices, the lordship of Sirius.

This is a warner of the same kind as the warners of old, and the Approaching Day has drawn near. The surah describes an audience that laughs instead of weeping, then drops the argument for a command to prostrate and worship.

themes.d: The surah defends the Prophet ﷺ as a witness and not an author, and its wording is about seeing and about whether the eye and the heart reported accurately. Who was seen has been disputed since the first generation: most commentators read verses 5 to 10 as Jibril, Aisha denied that he saw his Lord, and a different view is reported from Ibn Abbas.
The three goddesses and the female-named angels are treated as one error, a word inherited and repeated until it seemed to refer to something real.
That nobody carries another's load and that a person receives what he worked for are quoted from the oldest scriptures the surah names, presented as ancient rather than new.

themes.t: An ending that is an action
themes.d: The surah does not finish with a summary or a threat. It finishes with a command to prostrate and worship, which is why its recitation has always carried a prostration at the last verse.

heart: The first eighteen verses are among the few places in the Qur'an that describe what happened to the Prophet ﷺ himself, and on a slow reading their restraint is the thing to notice. Almost nothing is described. There is a distance, a covering that covered, a tree, and a repeated insistence that the sight was exact. What is preserved is the reliability of the witness rather than the vision itself.

The second half changes its subject to the reader without announcing it. Verse 32 forbids anyone to declare his own purity and mentions the womb in the same breath, dating a person's record earlier than any achievement he could cite. Verses 38 and 39 then remove every borrowed merit and leave a man holding only what he worked at.

passages.why: The denial that he speaks from desire, followed by the statement that it is revelation revealed: the surah's central claim in two short verses.
Idols reduced to names that people invented and then inherited. The method, attacking the word rather than the statue, is worth sitting with.
The prohibition on claiming purity for oneself, grounded in Allah's knowledge of a person from before he was born.
No bearer of burdens bears the burden of another, and man has nothing but what he strove for, quoted from the scriptures of Musa and Ibrahim.

connections.why: Al-Isra states the night travel to the Farthest Mosque in one verse, and An-Najm gives the sighting at the Lote Tree: together the two accounts a reader has.
At-Takwir also defends the Prophet ﷺ against the charge of madness and states that he saw the messenger on the clear horizon, in a different vocabulary.

virtue.text: An authentic prophetic practice is attached to this surah, not a merit promised to the reciter.
