Ibn Mas'ud reported that the Prophet ﷺ recited An-Najm and prostrated at its end, and that everyone present prostrated with him except one man who took a handful of dust and raised it to his face; the report is in Bukhari and Muslim. The schools differ on the recitation prostration generally, the Hanafis holding it obligatory and the others recommended, and that disagreement is not settled here.
virtue.src: prostration report from Ibn Mas'ud in Bukhari and Muslim; no virtue report

context: Al-Qamar is Makkan and opens by setting two statements side by side: the Hour has drawn near, and the moon has split. The splitting is reported in Bukhari and Muslim through several companions, among them Anas ibn Malik and Ibn Mas'ud, as a sign the people of Makkah had asked for and were given. Their response is quoted in the second verse, where they turn away and call it passing magic.

That response sets the surah's programme. If a sign shown in the sky can be dismissed within a verse, the argument has to come from history instead, so the rest recounts five peoples who dismissed the signs given to them. One sentence returns four times: We have made the Qur'an easy for remembrance, so is there any who will remember.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for the moon of its first verse, though reciters have long known it by its opening word as well, Iqtarabat, meaning it has drawn near. The two names point from opposite ends of time, one at an event that had happened and one at an event that had not.

movements.note: The Hour draws near, the moon splits, and the response is dismissal. The passage moves to the Day the Caller calls, when people come out of their graves with lowered eyes like scattered locusts.

Nuh is called mad and driven off, and prays that he has been overpowered; the sky opens, the earth bursts, and the waters meet upon a decree already fixed. 'Ad is given a howling wind that pulls people up like uprooted palm trunks.

Thamud objects that a single human being out of themselves should be followed. The camel is sent as a test and the water divided by turns, one man hamstrings her, and a single blast leaves them like dry sticks.
A storm of stones is sent and the family of Lut is saved before daybreak, described as the reward given to whoever is grateful, and the men who came demanding his guests have their eyes blinded.

movements.h: Fir'awn, and a warning to Makkah
movements.note: Fir'awn's people denied every sign and were seized, and the address turns on the Quraysh: are your disbelievers better than those, or do you rely on being an assembly that holds together.
The criminals are dragged on their faces, and three statements follow: everything was created by decree, His command is one word like the blink of an eye, and every small and great thing is written.

themes.t: A refrain that will not let the reader move on
themes.d: Four times the surah interrupts an account of destruction to say that the Qur'an has been made easy for remembrance, so the ease being claimed is asserted directly after the hardest material.
The surah opens with a sign given at the audience's own request and refused inside one verse. Everything afterwards treats refusal as the normal case, which is why the evidence offered is historical.

themes.t: Decree stated in the middle of consequence
themes.d: Verse 49 says that everything was created by measure, inside a surah otherwise occupied with people being held to account. Muslim records that these words came down when a group of Quraysh arrived arguing about the decree.
The verses are short, the rhyme regular, and the images compact enough to survive a single hearing, which fits its place in the two Eid prayers.

heart: Al-Qamar is built for the ear, and reading it slowly is a matter of letting the repetition work. Five peoples are dealt with in roughly forty verses, and the surah lingers over none of them. What lingers is the refrain, which returns after each account with the same words, so that by its fourth appearance a reader has begun answering it rather than hearing it.

The final verses are worth arriving at rather than reading on their own. After the locusts and the wind and the blast and the stones and the dragging on faces, the surah closes with gardens and rivers, and its last phrase names whose presence they are in: a Sovereign, Perfect in Ability.

passages.why: The Hour and the moon in one verse. What it reports is among the few signs the Quraysh saw with their own eyes.
The refrain in its first appearance, immediately after the flood, stating that the Qur'an has been made easy to remember and asking a question the reader is left holding.
The promise that the assembly will be defeated. 'Umar said he had wondered which assembly was meant, and at Badr saw the Prophet ﷺ reciting it as he put on his armour; the report is in Bukhari.
The closing verse, which locates the righteous by whose presence they are in rather than by what they have been given.

connections.why: The Prophet ﷺ recited Qaf and Al-Qamar together at both Eids. Qaf argues that the Hour will come; Al-Qamar shows what happened to those who waited for more proof.
Ash-Shu'ara runs through the same nations with a refrain of its own, but at length and with dialogue, so reading both shows what compression leaves out.

virtue.text: An authentic prophetic practice is attached to this surah, not a stated reward for reading it. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab asked Abu Waqid al-Laythi what the Prophet ﷺ used to recite at Eid al-Adha and Eid al-Fitr, and he answered that he recited Qaf and Iqtarabat as-Sa'ah, which is this surah; the report is in Sahih Muslim. That establishes where the surah was read and not a merit for the reciter.
virtue.src: Eid recitation from Abu Waqid al-Laythi in Muslim; no virtue report

context: Al-Waqi'ah is Makkan, and the traditional lists of the order of revelation place it in the middle of that period, when the dispute with Quraysh had narrowed to one question: whether a man who has become bones and dust is raised again. Their objection is quoted inside the surah itself at verse 47, in the words they used. Some early authorities held a few of its verses to be Madinan, and that matter is disputed.

The setting explains the surah's proportions. It opens with the event, sorts people into three groups within a few verses, then holds those groups in view for forty verses of physical detail before it argues with anyone. When the argument finally comes, it is about four ordinary things the deniers handled every day. A city that ruled out a second creation was still eating bread it had not made grow.
surahs.name_story: The name is a bare noun taken from the first verse: the thing that falls, the event that occurs. Nothing in it says what happens or to whom, and verse 2 adds only that there is no denying its occurrence. Naming a surah for an event while withholding any description of the event is part of how it argues, since the surah treats the fact as settled and spends its length on where a person will be standing.

movements.note: The Event falls, the earth is shaken, the mountains crumble until they scatter as dust. People are then sorted into three groups and named before any of them is described: the companions of the right, the companions of the left, and the foremost, who are also called those brought near.

The foremost are described first, on woven couches, served from a flowing spring, many of them from the earlier peoples and few from the later. The companions of the right receive a different inventory: thornless lote, clustered banana trees, spread shade, poured water, fruit neither cut off nor withheld.

Scorching wind, black smoke, shade that gives no relief, and the tree of zaqqum for food. Their state is traced back to what they had been: comfortable, fixed in the great sin, and saying the words quoted at verse 47.

movements.h: Four things they did not make
movements.note: The address turns to the living. The fluid a person comes from, the seed put into the ground, the water that falls from the cloud, the fire and the tree behind it. Each is named as something used rather than manufactured, and each is followed by the same question of who does the making.

movements.h: An oath, and what it swears to
movements.note: An oath by the positions of the stars, which the surah stops to call a mighty oath if they knew it. What it swears to is that this is a noble recitation, in a hidden book, touched by none but the purified.

movements.h: The throat, and the sorting again
movements.note: The dying scene, with the soul at the throat and the family looking on, unable to hold it. The three groups then return in three short passages, one outcome each, and the surah closes with the command to glorify that already stood at verse 74.

themes.d: Most passages on the Last Day divide people in two. This one adds a third and puts it first, and that third is defined by nearness rather than by which side its people are standing on.

themes.t: The argument from what is already in hand
themes.d: Verses 58 to 72 do not begin from the unseen. They begin from a seed and a fire, and the claim is that whoever did not make the first creation has no ground for ruling out the second.
Verse 82 says they made their provision to be that they deny. Denial is treated there as what a person does with what he receives, not as a conclusion he reasoned his way to.
The deathbed passage describes the one thing every listener has already watched happen to someone. There is no dialogue in it and no scene beyond a throat and a ring of people who cannot act.

heart: Recited slowly, the surah works by sorting. It names the three groups early, spends fifty verses filling each one with detail, then names them again at the end in passages that take seconds to read. A reader who has been inside the descriptions arrives at those closing lines already knowing what each name carries, which is what the repetition is for.

The passage that tends to stay is the one about dying. A throat, onlookers, and the statement that Allah is nearer to the man than they are while they cannot see it. The surah then asks them to send the soul back if they are able, and lets the silence stand as the answer. It ends by giving something to say rather than something to conclude.

passages.why: Two short questions about where a human being comes from, in the plainest words available. The Qur'an's case for the resurrection usually begins here, at the first creation rather than the second.
The farmer's verse. It grants the ploughing, denies the growing, and adds that the crop could be turned to dry chaff with a season's work left showing nothing.

The Book described as touched by none but the purified. Commentators differ over whether the purified are the angels who handle the preserved Book or people handling a copy, and the schools of law differ over what purity is required to touch a mushaf.
The soul reaching the throat while the family watches. Verse 85 states a nearness that nobody in the room can see, and these are lines readers return to at a bedside.

connections.why: Al-Haqqah names the Day with the same kind of bare noun and sorts people by the right and the left. It puts the record into the hand, which al-Waqi'ah never does, so the two give one scene from different angles.
Ar-Rahman stands immediately before it and covers much of the same ground in another key: ranked gardens, listed provisions, and a running question about things already given.

virtue.text: No authentic prophetic report establishes a specific merit for reciting al-Waqi'ah. The widely repeated saying that whoever recites it every night will never be touched by poverty is traced to Ibn Mas'ud and recorded by al-Bayhaqi in Shu'ab al-Iman and in similar collections; hadith critics have faulted its chain and it is commonly graded weak, so it is not given here as established. What the surah rests on is its content: the most detailed sorting of people at the resurrection anywhere in the Qur'an, and a closing command to glorify whose wording is echoed in the tasbih said while bowing in prayer.
virtue.src: no authentic virtue report; the poverty report traced to Ibn Mas'ud in al-Bayhaqi's Shu'ab al-Iman is commonly graded weak

context: Al-Hadid is Madinan, and the early authorities differ on when in that period it came. Verse 10 distinguishes those who spent and fought before the Conquest from those who did so after, and commentators differ over whether the Conquest named there is Hudaybiyyah or the taking of Makkah. A statement of Ibn Mas'ud recorded in Sahih Muslim about verse 16 has been read to place part of it earlier. What is not disputed is the audience: believers who had begun to own things.

That explains the surah's alternation. It moves between the largest statements it can make about Allah and the narrowest question it can put to a person, which is whether he will part with money. The wall passage at verses 12 to 15 and the rebuke at verse 16 name the danger directly, and it is not disbelief. It is hardness settling into people who already believe.
surahs.name_story: The surah takes its name from one word in verse 25, where iron is said to have been sent down, using the same verb used a few words earlier for the Book. Iron appears nowhere else in the surah. The naming fixes attention on that one sentence, which sets scripture, a balance and metal in a single line and states the purpose as people standing up for justice. What a reader is told by the name is that this surah thinks justice needs both a measure and a means.

movements.note: The opening tasbih, then a run of statements about Allah: the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, the One who knows what goes into the earth and what comes out of it, and who is with you wherever you are.

movements.h: Spend from what you hold in trust
movements.note: The command to spend from what you have been made successors over, and the offer of a loan to Allah that is returned multiplied. Those who gave before the Conquest are set above those who gave after, and both are promised good.

The believers with their light running ahead of them, and the hypocrites calling out to be waited for and told to go back and look for light elsewhere. A wall is then set between them with a gate in it, mercy inside and punishment outside.

A rebuke addressed to believers whose hearts have hardened as the hearts of earlier scripture-bearers hardened when long ages passed over them. Dead earth revived by rain is offered as the image of what is being asked of them.

This life given as play, amusement, adornment, mutual boasting and rivalry in wealth and children, followed by rain that pleases the growers and then yellows into debris. Then the register that holds every disaster before it happens, given so that no one despairs over what escapes him or exults over what he is handed.

Messengers sent with clear proofs, the Book and the balance sent down so people may uphold justice, and iron sent down with hard force and uses. Then Nuh, Ibrahim, and Jesus, whose followers invented a monasticism that was not prescribed for them, and a closing promise of two shares of mercy and a light to walk by.

themes.d: Verse 7 calls the addressees successors over their property, people it is passing through. The command to spend is presented as following from that description rather than as an added obligation.

The rebuke at verse 16 is aimed at believers, not deniers, and the cause it names is time. Earlier communities were given a book and then let the ages run on, and the same process is said to be under way.

Verse 25 puts proofs, a measure and metal into one sentence and says the point is to see who will support Him unseen. Justice is described as needing a standard and something hard enough to hold the standard in place.

themes.t: The register as the ground of steadiness
themes.d: Verses 22 and 23 give the decree with its purpose attached, and the purpose is practical: not to collapse over losses and not to be inflated by gains.

heart: The surah alternates between two scales, and slow recitation makes the alternation hard to miss. Verse 3 gives four names of Allah in a single clause. Verse 4 says He is with you wherever you are. Within a few verses of that, the subject is money, and the question is why anyone withholds it when the heavens and the earth are going to be inherited in any case.

Verse 16 is where readers tend to stop. It asks whether the time has not yet come for the hearts of those who believe to grow soft at the remembrance of Allah. Ibn Mas'ud's remark on it, recorded in Sahih Muslim, is that four years lay between their acceptance of Islam and this being said to them. Those are a companion's words about his own generation, and they set the interval at something short.

passages.why: Four names in one clause, with nothing added to explain them. Commentators have written at length on this verse and the verse itself does not.
The rebuke, addressed to people who already believe. It names the passing of time as the thing that does the damage, which is why it reads differently at forty than at twenty.
Worldly life summarised in five words, then the rain that pleases the growers before the crop yellows into debris. The word used for that debris is the same one al-Waqi'ah uses of the ruined harvest.
The register written before the event, followed immediately by the two things it exists to prevent. Despair and exultation are both named in the verse itself.

connections.why: Al-Hashr opens with the same tasbih and shows one concrete case of property changing hands under a rule. Al-Hadid argues in general terms for what al-Hashr legislates in a particular one.
At-Taghabun repeats the goodly loan and the framing of wealth and children as a test, in a shorter compass and without the historical setting, which makes the demand easier to see on its own.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting al-Hadid on its own. A report from al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah, recorded by Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, says the Prophet ﷺ used to recite the musabbihat before sleeping and said that among them is a verse better than a thousand verses; at-Tirmidhi graded it hasan gharib and later critics have questioned its chain. It names a group of surahs rather than this one and does not identify the verse, so nothing specific to al-Hadid is established by it. The surah's standing rests on its content, above all verses 16 and 25.
virtue.src: no surah-specific virtue report; the musabbihat report of al-'Irbad ibn Sariyah in Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi is general and its grading is disputed

context: Al-Mujadilah is Madinan, and its first verses answer one household. A woman came to the Prophet ﷺ about her husband, who had used the pre-Islamic formula of zihar, telling her she was to him as his mother's back. That formula put a wife outside the marriage without releasing her from it. The reports have her arguing her case and being told that nothing had come to him about her situation, and she raised the complaint to Allah. The early sources differ over her name, most often giving her as Khawlah bint Tha'labah, and her husband as Aws ibn as-Samit.

The opening verse states that her words were heard, and that statement sets the terms for everything after it. From one marriage the surah widens outward in stages: to counsel whispered in corners, to a greeting twisted at the door, to conduct inside the Prophet's ﷺ gathering, and finally to the division of people into two parties. Almost every subject it takes up is a form of speech, which is why it begins by establishing who is listening.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from verse 1, which describes the woman who disputes with the Prophet ﷺ about her husband. Some read it as al-Mujadalah, the dispute itself, rather than the woman who makes it. Either way, a surah of the Qur'an is named for an argument brought by a woman whose name the text does not give, and the argument is answered in the first line rather than deferred. Nothing in the naming softens the fact that she was pressing a case.

movements.h: The complaint, and the way out
movements.note: Her words are reported as heard. Zihar is declared a false statement, since the wives it speaks of are not mothers, and a way out is set in order: freeing a slave, then two consecutive months of fasting, then feeding sixty poor people. The jurists differ over the details of each option.

Those who set themselves against Allah and His Messenger are compared to earlier communities brought low. Then the verse that no three confer in secret without Him as the fourth, and no five without Him as the sixth, and no fewer or more, wherever they are.

A group forbidden from secret counsel goes back to it, and when they come to the Prophet ﷺ they bend the greeting into something Allah has not used. Such counsel is traced to Satan and said to be unable to harm the believers except by Allah's permission.

Make room in gatherings when asked, and those who believe and those given knowledge are raised in rank. Then the instruction to give charity before speaking privately with the Prophet ﷺ, and its removal a verse later, with prayer and zakah put in its place.

People who ally themselves with those Allah is angry at, and who use their oaths as a shield. The surah names two parties, Satan's and Allah's, and closes by saying that those who believe in Allah and the Last Day are not found loving those who oppose Him, even when they are fathers, sons, brothers or kin.

themes.t: A ruling given because a woman asked for one
themes.d: The law here arrives in answer to a specific complaint, and the surah keeps the order of events visible. The case comes first and the legislation follows it.
Verse 1 uses the verb for hearing three times before anything is legislated. Every later statement about whispered counsel and concealed intention rests on that opening claim.

themes.t: A cost instead of a dead end
themes.d: The pre-Islamic formula ended a marriage without dissolving it and left the wife suspended. The surah does not simply void the words; it attaches a price to them, and the schools of law differ on how that price is measured.
The last third moves from what people say to whom they stand beside, and it uses one word, party, for both sides. The surah treats loyalty as the place where speech finally shows what it was.

heart: The surah is about speech, and slow recitation makes the range of it audible: a woman's argument, a formula spoken by a husband in anger, counsel whispered between two men, a greeting bent into an insult, oaths held up as cover. Very little in it happens at a distance. Most of it happens in rooms, between people who know each other.

Verse 7 is the one that changes how the rest reads. It counts upward, three and then five, then stops counting and says fewer than that or more, placing Allah inside the group each time. Whatever a reader takes from the rulings on zihar or from the instruction about making room in a gathering, the surah has already established that no conversation has the number of participants it appears to have.

passages.why: The complaint is reported as heard before a single ruling is given. The placement is the point, and A'ishah's remark on the incident, recorded from her in the sunan collections, is that she herself was in the house and could not catch all of what the woman said.
The third option in the expiation, feeding sixty poor people, with a reason attached: so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger. The verse ends by calling these the limits set by Allah.
The verse on secret counsel. It counts three, then five, then stops counting and says fewer or more, placing Allah in the group each time.
Make room in gatherings when you are asked to. A small courtesy is given a verse of the Qur'an, and the verse ends with believers and those given knowledge raised in rank.

connections.why: Al-Ahzab states at verse 4 that the wives men declare to be like their mothers are not their mothers. Al-Mujadilah takes that same statement and attaches a procedure and a cost to it.

At-Talaq is the other Madinan surah that legislates a marital process step by step, and reading the two together shows the Qur'an handling the end of a marriage with waiting periods, witnesses and named obligations rather than a formula.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting al-Mujadilah. Its standing rests on what it records: a woman's complaint answered in the opening line, and the dismantling of a formula that had left wives neither married nor free. A remark of A'ishah about the incident, praising the hearing of the One whose hearing takes in all voices, is preserved from her in the sunan collections, but those are a companion's words and not a saying of the Prophet ﷺ.
virtue.src: no virtue report; A'ishah's remark on the occasion is a companion's statement recorded in the sunan collections

context: Al-Hashr is Madinan and was revealed about the expulsion of Banu an-Nadir, a Jewish tribe of the city, in the fourth year after the emigration. The sirah reports that the Prophet ﷺ went to them over a matter of blood money and that a plan was made to drop a stone on him from a roof, after which they were told to leave. They shut themselves in their strongholds. The siege lasted a matter of days and ended on terms: they would go, carrying what their camels could bear, leaving their weapons. Most settled at Khaybar and some went on to Syria.

Because there was no battle, the surah has a legal problem to solve, and it says so at verse 6: no horse or camel was spurred for this. Property taken without fighting could not be divided as spoils, so a separate rule is given, with its purpose stated before its list of recipients. The surah then turns from the property to the people receiving it, and the three groups it describes there are the reason this passage is read constantly outside its occasion.
surahs.name_story: The name is taken from verse 2, which calls the expulsion the first gathering. It records the act rather than the tribe, and it does so with a word the Qur'an uses elsewhere for the gathering at the resurrection, so the exile is set on a scale larger than itself. Sa'id ibn Jubayr reports that when he said to Ibn Abbas, Surat al-Hashr, Ibn Abbas told him to say Surat an-Nadir instead. That exchange is recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim, and both names have stayed in use.

movements.note: The opening tasbih, then the first gathering. They thought their strongholds would hold and were reached from a direction they had not considered, and they pulled down their own houses with their own hands and the hands of the believers. Verse 5 says the palms cut and the palms left standing were both by permission, and jurists have differed ever since over what may be destroyed in war.

movements.h: What is done with what is taken
movements.note: Property that came without a ride being spurred is assigned by rule, with the stated aim that it not stay circulating among the rich. Three groups are then named in turn: the emigrants who left their homes and property, the people of the city who love those who came to them, and those who come afterwards asking forgiveness for both.

movements.h: The promise that was not kept
movements.note: The hypocrites had told Banu an-Nadir they would leave with them and fight beside them, and did neither. Their fear of the believers is said to be greater than their fear of Allah, and their apparent unity is described as hearts pulled in different directions. The section ends with Satan telling a man to disbelieve and then disowning him.

movements.h: Look at what you sent ahead
movements.note: Every soul is told to consider what it has put forward for tomorrow. The warning that follows is against becoming like those who forgot Allah and were made to forget themselves, and the section closes by saying the people of the fire and the people of the garden are not equal.

Had this Qur'an come down on a mountain, the mountain would be seen humbled and split apart. The closing verses then run through the names of Allah without pause and end where the surah began, with everything in the heavens and the earth glorifying Him.

themes.d: The surah insists that nothing here was won by force and then builds a legal category on that fact. The rule for property taken without fighting differs from the rule for spoils, and the jurists differ over how it was to be allocated after the Prophet ﷺ died.

themes.t: Property described by where it must not settle
themes.d: Verse 7 gives the reason for the distribution before it gives the list of recipients, and the reason is that wealth should not become a thing turning over among the rich alone.

Verse 9 praises hosts who gave while they were short themselves, and the phrase it uses is that they prefer others over their own selves though poverty is their own condition. The verse is about the Ansar and reads as a standard.

themes.t: The Qur'an set against a mountain
themes.d: Verse 21 measures the book against a physical object so that its weight can be pictured, then says such comparisons are struck for people to think with.

heart: For a surah that begins with a siege, most of its length is spent somewhere else. Read slowly, the middle is a set of portraits: people who walked away from their property, people who took them in and preferred them to themselves while short of everything, and people who come long afterwards and ask forgiveness for both. By the surah's own arrangement a reader belongs to the third group, and verse 10 hands that group its words.

The last four verses are recited on their own more than any other part of it. Verse 21 sets the Qur'an against a mountain and says the mountain would split. The three that follow move through the names of Allah with no break in them, and the surah closes on the same tasbih it opened with, which leaves the whole exile framed at both ends by something larger.

passages.why: The account of the expulsion ends with an instruction to draw the lesson. Jurists cite this phrase when they argue that one case may be reasoned from another.

The rule for property taken without fighting, with its purpose stated inside the verse, and the clause about taking what the Messenger gives and refraining from what he forbids, which is among the verses most often cited for the authority of the sunnah.
The description of the Ansar, including the line about preferring others while in need themselves. It is a short verse and it sets a standard most readers measure themselves against rather than meet.
The closing three verses, a run of the names of Allah ending in tasbih. They are memorised early and recited apart from the surah by many readers.

connections.why: Al-Anfal legislates the division of what is taken in battle. Al-Hashr legislates what comes without a battle, and the two rules are deliberately different, which is why the surah insists no horse was spurred.
Al-Munafiqun gives a full portrait of the men who appear in verses 11 to 17 here, promising support to others that they never intend to deliver.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting al-Hashr. A report in at-Tirmidhi describes a reward for one who seeks refuge in a set form and then recites the closing three verses morning and evening; at-Tirmidhi himself called it gharib, and later hadith critics have graded its chain weak, so it is not offered here as established. What the surah rests on is its content: a rule of distribution with its purpose written into it, the description of the Ansar at verse 9, and the run of divine names at the end.
virtue.src: no established virtue report; the report on the closing verses in at-Tirmidhi is graded weak

context: Al-Mumtahanah is Madinan and belongs to the eighth year after the emigration, in the weeks before the march on Makkah. Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah, a man who had fought at Badr, wrote to Quraysh telling them of the preparations and sent the letter with a woman travelling south. The Prophet ﷺ sent Ali, az-Zubayr and al-Miqdad after her to a place called Rawdat Khakh; they overtook her and she produced the letter from her hair. Hatib said he had no clan in Makkah to shield his family and had wanted a favour owed to him there, not a change of religion. Umar asked to strike his neck, and the Prophet ﷺ said that he had been at Badr. The account is in al-Bukhari (3007) and Muslim.

That case shapes the whole surah. The man at the centre of it was not a disbeliever but a believer with relatives inside enemy territory, so what follows is about kinship under pressure rather than belief in the abstract. It is also why verses 7 to 9 arrive so quickly to qualify the opening prohibition, and why the last third deals with families split by the treaty: women arriving from Makkah, marriages ended, and dowries repaid.
surahs.name_story: The name comes from verse 10, where believing women who arrive from Makkah are to be examined before anything is decided about them. It is an odd choice, since the passage is short and sits near the end of the surah, and the name taken from it is passive: she who is examined. The naming settles attention on the woman whose claim was tested rather than on the men doing the testing, and it marks that section as the part of the surah that dealt with people rather than policy.

movements.note: Believers are told not to take Allah's enemy and their own as allies, offering them affection, when those people had driven out the Messenger and them. The section closes with the statement that neither relatives nor children will be of use on the Day of Resurrection, which answers Hatib's stated motive directly.

A good example is set in Ibrahim and those with him, who told their people plainly that they were free of them and of what they worshipped. One sentence is then taken out of the example, Ibrahim's promise to his father to seek forgiveness for him, followed by a prayer not to be made a trial for the deniers.

Allah may yet place affection between the two sides. He does not forbid kindness and fairness toward those who did not fight over religion and did not drive anyone from his home; what He forbids is allegiance to those who did. Some early authorities held verse 8 to have been abrogated and others held it in force, and the disagreement is old.

Believing women arriving from Makkah are to be examined, and if they are found believing they are not sent back, since the two sides are no longer lawful to each other. The marriages are ended, what the husbands paid is returned to them, and the same is owed in the other direction.

movements.h: The pledge, and the closing prohibition
movements.note: The terms on which the Prophet ﷺ is to accept the pledge of women, six clauses running from associating nothing with Allah to not disobeying in what is right. The surah then closes by repeating its prohibition on allying with a people who have earned Allah's anger and who have given up on the Hereafter.

themes.t: A named case rather than an abstract rule
themes.d: The prohibition arrives attached to a man whose motive was the safety of his relatives. That is why the surah says so much about kin, and why it does not read as a statement about strangers.

themes.t: The exception written into the example
themes.d: Verse 4 offers Ibrahim as a pattern and then withdraws one of his sentences from the pattern. The Qur'an rarely qualifies an example that precisely, and the qualification is placed inside the same verse.

Verse 7 raises the possibility of affection between the two sides before the surah explains how to behave in the meantime. Many of the people addressed as enemies here accepted Islam not long after the city was taken.

Verse 8 uses one verb for kindness and another for dealing justly, and applies both to those who did not fight and did not expel. It states what is not forbidden rather than what is commanded, which is a narrower claim than it is often made to carry.

heart: The surah is short and its subject is a line that runs through families. Recited slowly, it keeps returning to relatives: an enemy who is also kin, the statement that neither relatives nor children will help on the Day of Resurrection, Ibrahim telling his own people he is done with them, and the one sentence of Ibrahim's that is lifted out of the example because he said it to his father.

Verses 7 to 9 are where the surah adjusts its own weight. First the possibility that affection may yet be placed between the two sides. Then a statement of what is not forbidden, which is kindness and fairness toward those who did not fight over religion. A reader who takes the opening verse by itself will misread the surah, and it is the middle that prevents that.

passages.why: The prohibition with its cause given in the same breath: these are people who expelled the Messenger and those with him. The reason is historical and specific rather than a description of non-Muslims in general.
Ibrahim held up as an example, with one thing excluded from the example by name. It is worth reading twice for the exception alone.

The verse most quoted on dealing with non-Muslims who are not at war, with its two verbs. Some early authorities considered it abrogated and others did not, and this companion does not settle the question.

The terms of the pledge taken from women, listed one by one. The same terms appear in the reports of the pledges the Prophet ﷺ accepted, which makes this a rare case of a verse and a practice visible side by side.

connections.why: At-Tawbah states the disavowal of treaty-breakers at length and in severe terms. Read next to al-Mumtahanah, the two show the Qur'an separating those who fought and expelled from those who did neither.
Al-Fath records the treaty of Hudaybiyyah, whose clause about people crossing over to Madinah is what verses 10 and 11 here revise for the women who came.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting al-Mumtahanah. Its standing rests on what it settles and on how well the occasion is preserved: the case of Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah is recorded in al-Bukhari and Muslim, so a reader can see the exact situation the ruling answered. The surah is also the source of the terms on which the pledge of women was taken, which is why its last verses are quoted whenever that pledge is discussed.
virtue.src: no virtue report; the occasion is recorded in al-Bukhari (3007) and Muslim

context: As-Saff is Madinan and short. Verses 2 and 3 rebuke people for saying what they do not do, and the early accounts of the occasion differ: some connect the rebuke with men who spoke of what they would do in battle and then fell short, and one report in at-Tirmidhi's chapters of tafsir, from Abdullah ibn Salam, has a group of companions wishing to know which deed Allah loves most, with the surah sent down in answer. Since the accounts differ, the surah is better read for the situation it assumes than for any single incident.

What it assumes is a community about to be asked to hold a line, containing people whose words had run ahead of them. That is why it spends its middle on two earlier prophets who were injured by their own communities rather than by outsiders, and why verse 13 names help and a near conquest as something already in view. The whole is built like an address delivered before a march: a rebuke, two precedents, an offer, and a closing instruction.
surahs.name_story: The name is taken from verse 4, where Allah is said to love those who fight in His way in a row, as though they were a structure joined tight. It is a building word rather than a military one, and the simile puts the value on the joints instead of the individual parts. Naming the surah for it tells a reader that the subject is cohesion, and that the complaint in verses 2 and 3 about unkept words belongs to the same subject, since a line holds only if each person does the thing he said he would do.

movements.note: Everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah, and then, within two verses, the address narrows to the people listening and asks why they say what they do not do. The gap between the word and the deed is called greatly hateful in the sight of Allah.

The row joined like a firm structure, then Musa asking his people why they injure him when they know he was sent to them, and the statement that when they went crooked Allah let their hearts go crooked. Jesus follows, confirming the Torah before him and announcing a messenger to come after him by the name Ahmad.

The one who invents lies about Allah while being called to submission, and then the image of men trying to put out Allah's light with their mouths. The section answers itself with the statement that He sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth.

An offer stated in the language of commerce: belief and striving with wealth and lives, set against forgiveness, gardens and good dwellings. A second item is added that they are told they love, help from Allah and a conquest close at hand. The surah ends by telling them to be Allah's helpers as the disciples answered Jesus when he asked who would help him.

themes.t: Saying and doing as one subject
themes.d: The surah does not treat the gap between speech and action as a private fault. It sets the rebuke immediately before a verse about standing in ranks, where one man leaving his place is felt by the men beside him.

themes.t: A building word for a community
themes.d: The simile in verse 4 describes parts fitted so closely that nothing passes between them. What is praised is not the strength of any single person but the absence of gaps.
Musa and Jesus are both shown speaking to their own peoples, and the harm named in each case comes from within the community rather than from its enemies. The surah is addressing insiders throughout.

themes.t: An offer stated as a transaction
themes.d: Verses 10 to 13 name a price, a return and a term, and then add something that was not part of the bargain: help from Allah and a conquest close at hand.

heart: Fourteen verses, shaped like something said before an event rather than after it. The surah opens with the tasbih of the heavens and the earth, narrows within two verses to what one person says and does not do, then widens again to Musa and Jesus, both quoted while speaking to people who already knew who they were.

Verse 4 is the image the surah is named for, a row so closely fitted that a mason's word is used of it. Read after the rebuke that comes before it, that image explains why the rebuke was placed first. The last verse asks for the answer the disciples gave, and in Arabic that answer is three words long.

passages.why: Two verses on the distance between what a person says and what he does, with a strong word used for how that distance is regarded. They are short enough to hold in mind before speaking.
The row like a joined structure, and the source of the surah's name. The verse describes what Allah loves rather than what He commands, which is a different kind of statement.
Jesus confirming what came before him and naming a messenger to come after him. It is the most discussed verse in the surah and it is given in a single sentence.
The closing call to be Allah's helpers, quoting the disciples' reply to Jesus. The same reply appears in Al Imran, which makes the ending an echo rather than a new demand.

connections.why: Al Imran gives the same exchange between Jesus and the disciples at verse 52, inside a surah addressed to a community that had broken its ranks at Uhud.
At-Tawbah states the same transaction at verse 111, that Allah has bought from the believers their lives and their property, and it names the terms at greater length than As-Saff does.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting As-Saff. The report from Abdullah ibn Salam in at-Tirmidhi's chapters of tafsir describes an occasion of revelation rather than a merit for recitation, and the accounts of that occasion differ among the early authorities. What the surah rests on is its content: the rebuke at verses 2 and 3, the image of the joined row, and the announcement placed in the mouth of Jesus at verse 6.
virtue.src: no virtue report; the accounts of the occasion in the tafsir literature differ

context: Al-Jumu'ah is Medinan, addressed to a community that by then had a city, a market and a fixed weekly assembly. The Friday gathering was already in practice when the surah came down, which is why the surah does not introduce it but corrects the conduct around it. The closing verse has a well known occasion, recorded in Bukhari and Muslim from Jabir ibn Abdullah: a trade caravan reached Madinah while the Prophet ﷺ was on the pulpit, and the congregation went out to meet it until twelve men were left.

That setting explains a shape which otherwise looks like two surahs joined by accident. The first eight verses concern a people who were handed a Book and did not carry it. The last three concern a people handed a weekly summons who walked out of it. Placed in that order, the likeness of the donkey loaded with volumes stops being a remark about somebody else and becomes a warning set immediately before the Muslims' own test.
surahs.name_story: The surah takes its name from verse 9, the only place in the Qur'an where the day is named. Jumu'ah is built from the root for gathering, so the title names an assembly rather than a rite, and the surah treats it that way: what is legislated is not a form of words but an interruption. A reader who notices the naming will also notice that the community here is defined by what it is willing to stop doing.

movements.note: Everything in the heavens and the earth declares Allah free of imperfection. The surah moves at once to the sending of a Messenger ﷺ among the unlettered, with four tasks named in order: reciting the verses, purifying, teaching the Book, teaching wisdom.

movements.h: Those who have not yet joined
movements.note: The same sending is extended to others who have not yet caught up with the first generation. The whole matter is then called the bounty of Allah, given to whom He wills.

The likeness of the donkey loaded with volumes is applied to those given the Torah who then did not carry it. A claim of exclusive alliance with Allah is met with a test, to wish for death if the claim is true, followed by the note that the death being fled will meet them anyway.

movements.h: The call, the dispersal, the caravan
movements.note: The command is short: when the call is made on Friday, hasten to the remembrance and leave the sale. Verse 10 releases the congregation back into the market as explicitly as verse 9 called them out of it, and verse 11 records what happened when a caravan arrived during the sermon.

themes.d: Verse 5 turns on a verb about bearing a load. A scripture can be preserved, recited and defended without being carried, and the surah measures a community by that distance rather than by its possession of the text.
Nothing in the Friday command asks for withdrawal from work. It fences off one hour, and its whole weight falls on the fact that the hour arrives while business is open.

Verses 6 to 8 do not dispute a doctrine. They propose a test of sincerity anyone could apply to himself, on the reasoning that a claim to exclusive friendship with Allah should show up in the attitude to dying.

themes.t: A messenger for people not yet arrived
themes.d: Verse 3 attaches later comers to the same sending. It is the line that makes the surah's address current rather than historical, without claiming that later generations stand where the first stood.

heart: Recited slowly, the pairing in verses 9 and 10 is what stays. One sentence pulls a person out of the market and the next sends him back into it, and neither is more emphatic than the other. The surah is not asking for a changed life. It asks for a changed position during a fixed hour, repeated every week, which is harder to keep than one large sacrifice.

Verse 5 is the difficult one to sit with, because it is not addressed to the reader and describes exactly the reader's own exposure. The animal in the image is not accused of anything. It is carrying something of value and has no access to it, and nowhere does the surah suggest the load is worthless.

passages.why: The four tasks of the Messenger ﷺ named in sequence, and close to the list Ibrahim asked for in 2:129. Reading the two together shows a request made in one era and answered in another.
The likeness of one who carries volumes without carrying what is in them. It is the surah's sharpest sentence and the easiest to aim at other people.
The two commands as a pair. Most readers know the first half, and the second half, which sends people out to seek provision, is what keeps the first from becoming withdrawal.
A verse that names an actual failure of an actual congregation and preserves it. What is with Allah is better than diversion and than trade, said to people who had just demonstrated the opposite.

connections.why: As-Saff opens with the same glorification and also raises a community that received a prophet and did not hold to him. It offers a trade that saves from a painful punishment, which sets up the ordinary trade that empties the mosque at the end of Al-Jumu'ah.
The Prophet ﷺ recited the two together in the Friday prayer, and they show one congregation from two sides: those who leave for a caravan, and those who stay and mean nothing by it.

virtue.text: The Prophet ﷺ recited Al-Jumu'ah in the Friday prayer, with Al-Munafiqun in the second unit. This is recorded in Sahih Muslim in the Book of the Friday Prayer, in Abu Hurayrah's report (877) and again in Ibn Abbas's (879). A second pairing, Al-A'la with Al-Ghashiyah, is authentically recorded in the same chapter from an-Nu'man ibn Bashir, so the practice was not fixed to a single choice. What these reports establish is a practice of the Prophet ﷺ, not a stated reward, and no authentic report attaches a specific merit to reciting this surah outside that prayer.
virtue.src: Sahih Muslim 877 and 879, Book of the Friday Prayer

context: Al-Munafiqun is Medinan and belongs to the return from the campaign against Banu al-Mustaliq. A quarrel at a watering place had set emigrants against helpers, and Abdullah ibn Ubayy said that once they were back in Madinah the more honoured would drive out the more humble. Zayd ibn Arqam, then a boy, heard it and reported it. Ibn Ubayy swore he had said nothing, the report was set aside, and Zayd was left in a distress he later described. The surah came down naming what had been said, and the Prophet ﷺ told him that Allah had confirmed him. The account is recorded in Bukhari.

The setting explains why so much of the surah is portraiture rather than argument. The people described were not opponents outside the city but attenders inside it, who pronounced the testimony aloud and who looked and spoke well. That is why verse 4 concedes their appearance instead of denying it, and why the surah ends by turning to the believers with the material hypocrisy is made from: wealth and children taking the place of remembrance.
surahs.name_story: Named for a group of people rather than for a subject, a scene or an oath. The Qur'an takes titles from cattle, bees and the dawn, and this one from a class of men inside the Muslim community, which fixes both the surah's address and its difficulty. The naming also fixes the tense. It does not say the deceivers of Madinah, it names a condition, and the last three verses make plain that readers are expected to check themselves against it.

movements.h: The testimony and the propped timber
movements.note: They say what is true while lying, and their oaths serve as cover. Verse 4 grants that their forms please the eye and their speech holds attention, then compares them to lengths of timber leaned against a wall, and notes that they take every shout as aimed at them.

Invited to come so that the Messenger ﷺ might ask forgiveness for them, they turn their heads away. The following verse states that the asking will not help them, which is the hardest line in the surah.

movements.h: Two sentences that were actually said
movements.note: The order to withhold spending until the people around the Messenger ﷺ disperse, and the boast about the honoured expelling the humble. Each is answered by relocating what is being claimed: the treasuries belong to Allah, and so does honour.

The address changes. Wealth and children are named as what diverts from remembrance, spending is commanded before death arrives, and the surah closes on a man asking for a short delay so that he might give charity, and not receiving it.

themes.t: A true sentence from a lying witness
themes.d: Verse 1 does not contest the words. It contests the witness, and sets Allah's testimony against theirs. Truthfulness in the Qur'an belongs to a person before it belongs to a statement.

Polemic normally makes its targets ugly. This surah admits that their bodies please the eye and their talk is worth listening to, which is what makes the warning usable: the community is told in advance that it will find them convincing.
They think every shout is against them. The line describes a permanent state of exposure produced by the position itself, not by anything the believers were doing to them.

themes.t: The diagnosis handed to the healthy
themes.d: The last three verses drop the subject and speak to those who believe. Placing that warning here rather than elsewhere treats preoccupation with property and family as the raw material out of which the first eight verses are built.

heart: This is a short surah with an uncomfortable design, and slow recitation is what exposes it. Eight verses describe people the reader is confident he is not, and then verse 9 turns and speaks to him directly about his wealth and his children. Nobody reads the first part expecting the second.

Verse 10 sets a scene instead of issuing a rule. A man asks for a brief postponement so that he might give something away and be counted among the righteous. Nothing in the request is extreme and nothing in the answer is harsh, since it only states that no soul is delayed once its term has come.

passages.why: The testimony is word for word correct, and the same verse calls the speakers liars. The clearest statement in the Qur'an that a sentence and its speaker are judged separately.
The propped timber, and the admission that comes just before it. Worth returning to whenever impressiveness is being treated as evidence.
The point at which the surah changes audience. A warning about wealth and children placed at the end of a description of hypocrisy is not an unrelated appendix.
The request for a delay and the flat refusal. Two verses that put a limit on every intention being kept for later.

connections.why: The Prophet ﷺ paired them in the Friday prayer, and they belong together beyond the pairing: one shows a congregation leaving for a caravan, the other a congregation that stays and means nothing by it.

At-Tawbah treats the same group at far greater length at Tabuk, with their excuses, their oaths and the mosque they built to divide. Al-Munafiqun compresses into eleven verses what At-Tawbah spreads over many pages.

virtue.text: The Prophet ﷺ recited Al-Munafiqun in the second unit of the Friday prayer, after Al-Jumu'ah. It is recorded in Sahih Muslim in the Book of the Friday Prayer, from Abu Hurayrah (877) and from Ibn Abbas (879). The report establishes a practice and not a reward. No authentic prophetic report attaches a specific merit to reciting this surah, and its weekly place in that prayer is the whole of what is soundly established about it.
virtue.src: Sahih Muslim 877 and 879, Book of the Friday Prayer

context: At-Taghabun is usually counted Medinan, though the early authorities differ over it and some hold part of it Makkan, so the period is best given as disputed. It is the last of the surahs that open by declaring that everything in the heavens and the earth glorifies Allah. One occasion reported for verse 14, transmitted from Ibn Abbas, concerns men of Makkah whose wives and children held them back from emigrating and who later wanted to punish them for it.

Whatever the setting, the surah's movement runs from the largest frame to the smallest. It begins with dominion and creation, passes through the destruction of earlier peoples and the denial of resurrection, names the Day of Assembly, and then spends its last five verses inside a household: a family that obstructs, property that tests, an instruction to fear Allah as much as one is able. That compression is the argument. Domestic strain is placed in the same frame as the resurrection rather than in a smaller one.
surahs.name_story: Taghabun comes from ghabn, the loss taken by whichever party came off worse in an exchange. The word belongs to the market, and verse 9 attaches it to the Day of Assembly: that is the Day of Taghabun, of mutual loss and gain. Naming the resurrection with a trader's word implies that a life was a transaction whose terms were agreed while it was being lived, and whose balance is read once, in public, at the end.

movements.h: Dominion, and two kinds of people
movements.note: Everything glorifies Allah, and the surah moves immediately to the fact that He created every person, and that among them is a denier and among them is a believer. He shaped them, perfected their forms, and knows what is inside the chest.

Earlier peoples refused messengers on the grounds that they were human beings. The denial of resurrection is answered by an oath the Prophet ﷺ is told to swear, and the passage closes by commanding belief in Allah, His Messenger and the light sent down.
The assembly is named and the two outcomes are stated: misdeeds removed and gardens entered, or the Fire and permanence in it.
The verse on affliction is followed not by an explanation but by a promise about the heart. Obedience is commanded, and the Messenger's ﷺ responsibility is limited to clear delivery.

Spouses and children are named as capable of being enemies, and pardon is commanded in the same verse. Then property as a trial, taqwa to the limit of ability, protection from one's own stinginess, and the loan given to Allah.

themes.t: The division runs through the crowd
themes.d: Verse 2 says He created you and then splits the created in the same sentence. Neither side of the split is given a nation, an era or a lineage, which is unusual for a verse about disbelief.

In three places the Qur'an tells the Prophet ﷺ to answer the denial of resurrection with an oath rather than a further proof. Verse 7 is one of them, and the form marks the point where argument has been exhausted and declaration takes over.

It does not say the affliction will lift or that a reason will be supplied. It says the heart of one who believes will be guided, which is an offer about the person rather than about the circumstance.

Fear Allah as much as you are able stands beside the demand in 3:102 to fear Him as He should be feared. Commentators have long discussed how the two relate, and the wording here is the one addressed to people already under strain.

heart: The surah is unusually plain about family. Verse 14 states that among a man's wives and children are enemies to him and then, without a break, tells him to pardon, overlook and forgive. It does not reconcile the two halves or explain how both can be true at once. Anyone reciting it during a bad stretch at home will find the verse holding both facts and softening neither.

Verse 11 is what most people carry away. It gives no account of why the thing happened and makes no promise that it will end. What it offers is narrower and steadier: permission is not absence, and a heart can be guided while the circumstance stands exactly where it stood.

passages.why: The verse the surah is named from. It gives the resurrection a commercial name and then, in the same breath, states what removes a person's misdeeds.
The verse people reach for after bad news, and it repays a careful reading, since the promise attached is about the heart rather than about the event.
Enemies inside the household and the command to pardon them, in one sentence. Few verses set a difficulty and its treatment this close together.
Taqwa measured by capacity, followed by success defined as being guarded from one's own greed. The pairing is the surah's practical summary.

connections.why: Al-Hadid opens with the same glorification, uses the same image of a goodly loan given to Allah, and sets the decree of hardship beside the command to spend. The two surahs work the same material at different lengths.

Both close on wealth and children as the thing that diverts, and both follow with an order to spend before the term expires. Read one after the other, the same closing argument arrives twice, once at the end of a description of hypocrisy and once at the end of a description of the resurrection.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting At-Taghabun. A report that the Prophet ﷺ used to recite the musabbihat, the surahs that open with glorification, before sleeping is transmitted by Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi from al-Irbad ibn Sariyah, but its grading is discussed and it concerns the group rather than this surah, so nothing particular to At-Taghabun follows from it. What the surah rests on is its content: verse 11 on affliction and verse 16 on the limits of ability are among the most cited verses in the Qur'an on hardship, and their standing does not depend on a virtue report.
virtue.src: no established virtue report; the musabbihat report in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi is general and its grading is discussed

context: At-Talaq is Medinan and came after the divorce legislation of Al-Baqarah was already in force, which is why it supplements rather than begins. The occasion most often cited is the divorce Ibn Umar pronounced while his wife was menstruating. The Prophet ﷺ ordered him to take her back, keep her until she was pure, and divorce her at that point if he still wished. The report is in Bukhari and Muslim, and the ruling turns on the surah's opening instruction, that divorce is to be pronounced with reference to the counted period.

This is legislation written for the moment a marriage is ending badly, and its structure answers that. It fixes a time, since the waiting period is counted from a defined point rather than begun at random. It fixes a place, since she is not to be put out of the house and is not to leave it. It fixes money, in lodging, maintenance during pregnancy and a wage for nursing. Between those clauses the surah keeps inserting a line about fearing Allah and what follows from it, and that alternation of ruling and assurance is the design of the whole.
surahs.name_story: The surah is named for the act it regulates, which is itself a statement: a whole surah is given to the ending of marriages, and the ending is handled as a procedure with limits rather than as a private decision. Ibn Mas'ud called it the shorter Surah of Women, setting it beside An-Nisa, and his remark is recorded in Bukhari. Those are a companion's words and not a prophetic naming, but they describe the relation between the two surahs accurately.

movements.h: Time, place, and the two exits
movements.note: Divorce is pronounced with reference to the counted period, which is then to be counted. She is not put out of her house and does not leave it. At the end of the term two lawful outcomes remain, retention or separation, both required to be done decently and before two just witnesses, and the passage ends with the first assurance: whoever fears Allah is given a way out.

Provision arrives from a direction not reckoned on, and whoever relies on Allah is sufficed. The waiting periods follow for women past menstruation, for those who have not menstruated, and for the pregnant, whose term ends at delivery. Verse 5 closes with misdeeds removed and reward enlarged.

House them where you house yourselves, according to your means, and do not harm them in order to make their position untenable. Pregnancy is provided for until delivery, nursing is paid for, and a man spends from what he has been given and is not charged beyond it.

The surah breaks off from family law to a town that defied its Lord's command and was called to a severe account. The turn is abrupt, and it ends by addressing people of understanding who believe, with the statement that a reminder has been sent down to them.

movements.h: The Messenger, and the seven heavens
movements.note: That reminder is identified as a Messenger ﷺ reciting clear verses to bring people out of darknesses into light. The final verse widens to seven heavens and the like of them of earth, with the command descending among them.

themes.t: The clauses restrain the stronger party
themes.d: Almost every instruction limits what the husband may do. He may not expel her, may not use hardship to squeeze her out, may not withhold what he is able to give. Legislation of this kind is written against whoever holds the power to act.

Three times the surah stops a procedural instruction to say what comes to whoever fears Allah. The promises are not gathered into a separate passage, and their placement inside the driest stretch of the surah is deliberate.

Verse 1 supplies a reason and not only a duration: you do not know, perhaps Allah will bring about after that a new matter. The interval is built to leave room for a reversal neither party can currently picture.

The provisions on lodging and maintenance are the ground of a long disagreement about what is owed to a woman divorced irrevocably. Some hold she receives both lodging and maintenance, some lodging alone, some neither, and the dispute turns partly on the report of Fatimah bint Qays. This companion records the disagreement and does not settle it.

heart: Law is not usually what a person recites for steadiness, and this surah is the exception because of where its consolation sits. The promise of a way out and of provision from an unreckoned direction is not placed in a passage about trust in Allah. It arrives in the middle of instructions about witnesses and waiting periods, spoken to two people whose marriage has just failed, which is to say at the point where a way out is hardest to picture.

The other thing slow recitation makes visible is how much of this surah concerns a dwelling. Her house in verse 1. Where you yourselves live, in verse 6. A prohibition on making the place unbearable so that she leaves of her own accord. The surah keeps returning to a door and to a woman who is not to be pushed through it.

passages.why: The prohibition on expelling her, with the reason given at the end: perhaps Allah will bring about after that a new matter. The most hopeful sentence in the Qur'an's divorce legislation, addressed to the man who has just pronounced it.

The most quoted verses of the surah, and almost always quoted away from their setting. Restored to it, the way out and the unreckoned provision are being promised to someone in the middle of a divorce.
Housing, the prohibition on harming her to constrain her, and payment for nursing. It reads like a checklist because that is what it is.

Spending measured by what a man has been given, with the statement that Allah does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it. This is what keeps the surah's financial obligations from becoming a second injury.

connections.why: Al-Baqarah carries the main body of the law, including the waiting periods, the two pronouncements and the conditions for return. At-Talaq assumes all of it and adds the cases left open, so the two are read as one file.

An-Nisa is the longer Surah of Women that Ibn Mas'ud's name for this surah refers to, and it approaches marital breakdown from the other end: arbitration between the two, reconciliation, and what is owed when a marriage is kept rather than ended.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting At-Talaq. Its standing rests on what it contains rather than on a reward attached to reciting it: this is one of very few surahs given over almost entirely to a single field of law, and the rulings in it underlie an entire chapter of fiqh. Reports circulate assigning rewards to individual surahs and many of them are weak or forged, and nothing sound assigns one here.
virtue.src: no established virtue report

context: At-Tahrim is Medinan and was revealed about an episode inside the Prophet's ﷺ own household. He had made something lawful forbidden to himself in order to please his wives, and the first verse addresses that directly. Accounts of what the thing was differ. The one recorded in Bukhari and Muslim, from Aisha, concerns honey he used to drink at the house of one of his wives, after which two of them agreed to tell him they detected an unpleasant smell on him, so he resolved not to drink it again. Another account, that the matter concerned Mariyah, is reported elsewhere and is disputed. The Qur'an itself does not name it.

The surah's audience widens in stages, and this is what the setting explains. It opens with the Prophet ﷺ, narrows to two of his wives, opens again to all who believe, addresses those who disbelieve on the Day of Judgment, and closes on four women, none of them from this community. The household matter is finished by verse 9 and then dropped. The last three verses answer it from a different direction, by asking what a marriage actually secures and showing that it secures nothing either way.
surahs.name_story: The name is taken from the verb in the first verse, the making of a thing forbidden. It is an unusual title, since it is drawn not from a command the surah issues but from an act the surah questions, and the act was the Prophet's ﷺ own. That this correction was recited, memorised and transmitted by the community he was leading is part of what the surah tells a reader about the text: nothing was removed from it to protect the man who delivered it.

movements.note: The opening question is put to the Prophet ﷺ about forbidding himself what Allah had made lawful in order to please his wives. Verse 2 states that Allah has already ordained the release from such oaths.

Something told in confidence to one wife reached another. He was informed of it, and disclosed part while passing over part, which the surah records exactly. The two are then called to turn back, since their hearts had inclined, and told what would follow if they backed each other against him.

The address opens to all believers with a command concerning a Fire whose fuel is people and stones and over which stand angels who do not disobey what they are ordered. Verse 7 turns to the deniers on that Day and refuses their excuses in advance.

Believers are called to a repentance described as nasuh, with the promise of a Day on which the Prophet ﷺ and those with him are not disgraced, their light running ahead of them while they ask for it to be completed. Verse 9 instructs the Prophet ﷺ to strive against the deniers and the hypocrites.

Two examples of disbelief, the wives of Nuh and Lut, who were under two righteous servants and were not helped by it. Two of belief, the wife of Pharaoh, who asked for a house near Allah, and Maryam, who confirmed the words of her Lord.

themes.t: A correction kept in the record
themes.d: The first verse questions a decision of the Prophet ﷺ, and the community that revered him preserved it inside the text he taught them. Nothing about the episode was smoothed away, and the survival of this surah is itself an argument about how the Qur'an reached its readers.

themes.t: What a household does not secure
themes.d: The two condemned women were married to prophets. Of the two praised, one was married to the worst tyrant the Qur'an names and the other was not married at all. Proximity settles nothing in either direction.

Verse 6 makes a person answerable beyond himself, and the verb it uses is protective rather than punitive. What is asked for is guarding, which is why the command does not sit oddly at the close of a domestic quarrel.

The verse calls for tawbah nasuh and leaves it undefined, and commentators supply several definitions. The verse supplies an outcome instead, ending on believers asking for their own light to be completed rather than on a list of conditions.

heart: Slow recitation makes the surah's velocity plain. In the space of a dozen verses it moves from a disagreement about honey to a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, and then back into a house. Anyone who has had a bad week at home will notice that the Qur'an did not treat a domestic episode as beneath its attention, and did not treat it as small either.

Verse 11 is spoken inside a palace by a woman whose husband was killing people for believing what she believed. She asks for a house near Allah before she asks to be saved from Pharaoh. The order of the two requests is what makes the verse hold, since the first thing she wanted was not an escape.

passages.why: The verse that turns a private episode into a general responsibility. It is the standard proof text for a person's duty toward his household and it is worded as protection rather than as authority.
The call to a repentance that is sincere, and the du'a at the end of it, that our Lord complete our light for us and forgive us. Worth returning to when repentance has become repetitive.
Two women married to prophets, and neither marriage helped them. The clearest statement in the Qur'an that closeness to a righteous person is not a defence.
Asiyah's request. The house comes first and the rescue second, and the force of the verse is entirely in that order.

connections.why: Al-Ahzab addresses the Prophet's ﷺ wives directly, gives them a choice between the world and Allah with His Messenger, and sets the standard that At-Tahrim then applies to one incident. The two are read together for the reason a rule and a case are.
At-Tahrim closes on Maryam in a single verse that assumes the reader knows the rest. Surah Maryam supplies what is assumed, so reading it after this one fills in the woman the last verse only names.

virtue.text: No authentic report establishes a specific merit for reciting At-Tahrim. What is authentically recorded about it is the occasion behind its opening, in Bukhari and Muslim from Aisha, and Umar's long account of the same period, which is also in the two collections. Those establish the setting and not a reward for recitation. The surah's standing rests on the correction it preserves and on the four examples it ends with.
virtue.src: no established virtue report; occasion reports in Bukhari and Muslim

context: Al-Qalam is Makkan and belongs to the earliest stretch of the revelation. The traditional lists usually place it second, immediately after Al-'Alaq, though they do not fully agree and the ordering of the first few surahs is not settled. The charge it answers was being made in public and was specific: that the man delivering this was majnun, out of his mind. Verse 2 denies it before anything else is said, and the denial is placed under an oath sworn by the pen.

That charge explains the surah's method, which is comparison rather than defence. It does not set out to prove the Prophet's ﷺ sanity. It states his character, asks which of the two parties will turn out to be the afflicted one, supplies a portrait of the accuser, and then tells a story about men whose reasonable plan was cancelled between one night and one morning. By the time the accusation reappears in verse 51, it has been left standing next to the people making it.
surahs.name_story: The title comes from the oath in the first verse, by the pen and what they inscribe. Putting writing at the head of a surah revealed to a man who did not write, in a city that ran on memory and speech, is a deliberate placement, and the same instrument appears in Al-'Alaq among the very first verses revealed. A reader who notices that will read the opening as one move: the answer to a rumour is an oath sworn by the means of permanent record.

movements.h: By the pen, and the charge denied
movements.note: The oath, the denial that he is possessed, an uninterrupted reward, and the statement that he is upon a great character. Verses 5 and 6 promise that both sides will see which of them is the afflicted one, which turns an insult into a question with a scheduled answer.

An instruction not to yield to the deniers, with the note that they want him to soften so that they may soften in return. A run of descriptions of one opponent follows, covering habitual oath swearing, slander carried between people, obstruction of good, cruelty, and a word rendered variously as ignoble or as one attached to a family not his own. His confidence is traced to his wealth and his sons, and the passage ends with a mark to be branded on his nose.

Men swore they would harvest at first light and made no exception for the will of Allah. Their crop was struck in the night, they set out early telling each other to keep the poor out, and they arrived at a blackened ruin. The one among them who had warned them speaks, they turn on one another, and they end by hoping for a better exchange from their Lord.

movements.h: A run of demands for evidence
movements.note: The righteous have gardens, and the question is put whether those who submit will be treated like the criminals. A series of demands follows: produce the scripture, the sworn undertaking, the partners, the knowledge of the unseen on which the assumption rests. Verses 42 and 43 set a Day when they are called to prostrate and cannot, and the wording of verse 42 has been read in more than one way by the commentators.

movements.h: Patience, and the man in the fish
movements.note: The Prophet ﷺ is told to wait for his Lord's decision and not to be like the companion of the fish, who called out while choked with grief. Had a favour from his Lord not reached him he would have been cast on the bare shore blamed, and his Lord chose him instead. The surah ends where it began, with the word majnun in their mouths and the reply that this is only a reminder to the worlds.

themes.d: Nothing here argues for the Prophet's ﷺ sanity on evidential grounds. The surah asks which side is the afflicted one and then produces the evidence about the other side, which is a stronger position than a denial.

Verse 4 makes character the proof, a claim anyone in Makkah could test against forty years of observation. Aisha, asked later about his character, answered that it was the Qur'an, in a report recorded in Sahih Muslim.

The men in the parable were not cruel by intention until the morning, they were confident. Their whole failure begins with an oath sworn about tomorrow without the exception that Allah may decide otherwise.

Verses 44 and 45 describe being drawn on by stages from a direction not noticed, and time being extended. Delay is presented as an active way of dealing with people rather than as inattention, which answers why nothing had yet befallen the accusers.

heart: This is the surah for the period when someone else's account of a person has become the public account. Its opening does not console by reassurance. It changes the ranking instead: the reward is uninterrupted and the character is great, and both are stated before the accusation has even been examined, which is a different kind of steadiness from being told that a rumour will pass.

The closing movement is where recitation slows without being asked to.
